Our analysis utilizes a dataset comprising near-infrared 2MASS photometry and K2 or Kepler photometry in the B band from 1,300 microlensed giant stars. By constructing a theoretical spectral atlas, we identified a distinct absorption feature in the NIR spectrum of giant stars: a broad peak near 1.2 micrometers. This feature corresponds to the fundamental vibrational transition of CO. We demonstrate that the peak's height and width serve as precise indicators of stellar atmospheric $T_{\rm eff}$ and $(t_{\rm eff}, \log{g})$. Furthermore, we examine evolutionary trends in $(t_{\rm eff}, \log{g})$ across the bulge using our stellar parameters, offering insights into the evolution of the intense intensity bump at 1.1 micrometers. Additionally, we analyze the evolutionary path of giants on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, focusing on the recently proposed "pre-AGB valley." We confirm its existence in the bulge and utilize high-resolution MUSE observations of the Galactic center to investigate the valley's origin. Finally, we address recent discussions regarding the future pulsation characteristics of bulge giants.

We demonstrate that the recently identified pre-AGB valley represents incomplete stellar evolution rather than marking the transition to the AGB. Specifically, we show that the majority of stars in this valley are actually moving toward the RGB, indicating that valley stars have not yet evolved toward the AGB. Consequently, it appears highly unlikely that a distinct pulsation regime exists separating these two groups. Furthermore, we investigate whether stellar rotation could explain the valley's presence. This topic requires further research, particularly concerning whether rotation-induced variability explains the lack of pulsators in the bulge. Lastly, we explore recent debates regarding future pulsation regimes in bulge stars. Our findings indicate that valley stars may pulsate in the Baade's window region, though confirming pulsation in any pulsation regime remains challenging. In conclusion, the valley signifies incomplete evolution, offering valuable insights into the internal structure of stars as they transition between the main sequence and the AGB. Furthermore, valley stars provide excellent tracers for the bulge's stellar orbital dynamics. Finally, because the valley is most prominent in metal-rich environments, it serves as a valuable tool for studying metallicity gradients in galaxies.

Focusing on the scenario where only one of these singlets is very light, we demonstrate how the light singlet can induce significant corrections to the masses of both lighter singlet and heavier doublet Higgs bosons through neutrino singlet-triplet-couplings. These interactions also yield significant radiative corrections to the lightest doublet Higgs boson mass, potentially elevating it to approximately 600 GeV. Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has garnered significant interest recently, yet the field lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework to guide architectural design. Current research on FL systems is fragmented into isolated efforts, making it difficult to compare their strengths and limitations. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a theoretical framework for Federated Learning architecture. Subsequently, we apply this framework to classify all prior FL research and identify potential improvements for future developments.

This study addresses dynamic scheduling in large-scale NDN-based systems by employing utility maximization within a min-max framework. We analyze computing scenarios involving both static and access-delay-aware scheduling, developing corresponding analytical and control methods with specified error margins. Consequently, there is a growing need for access-delay-aware and robust service scheduling strategies. First, despite experimental validations, many studies lack formal security guarantees because they fail to rigorously define the adversary's capabilities. Specifically, the power of adversarial examples is often improperly bounded by restricting access to the target agent's policy or rewards, or by limiting modifications to training data points closest to the attacked trajectory. Second, current approaches primarily focus on episodic RL tasks like Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and objective optimization, leaving substantial theoretical groundwork unestablished. This lack of formal foundations hinders a clear definition of security guarantees and makes it difficult to determine which properties are essential for generalizing to novel environments. In this work, we address these issues by formulating powerful, provably effective adversarial attacks against RL agents. We begin by identifying fundamental constraints on adversarial models based on their access to agent information, a perspective that clarifies model definitions and their implications for security. Building on this, we introduce two general, practically relevant, and formally grounded adversarial models. For each model, we develop and analytically verify corresponding adversarial examples, and in all cases, we construct provably safe environments. Extensive experiments across standard RL benchmarks support our claims. Notably, in complex simulated robotic driving tasks involving deep RL agents, we demonstrate that even a marginally more complex adversarial model can successfully deceive the target agent. Our code is available at https://github.com/zeyu-wei/rl-security.git.

utilizing an entropic risk measure within episodic, non-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs). We introduce ALGO, a novel, simple, and efficient algorithm designed for this context. Under non-stationary conditions, ALGO maintains a collection of virtual policies grounded in the instantaneous conditional risk aversion (CRA) property. For stationary MDPs, these virtual policies converge to a single policy that achieves near-optimal performance with high probability. In the non-stationary setting, ALGO delivers effective approximation guarantees regarding dynamic risk and regret. Specifically, in non-stationary episodic MDPs with the constant CRA condition, we derive bounds of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ for both regret and dynamic risk, where $K$ represents the episode length and $T$ denotes the total runtime. Additionally, we extend these bounds to scenarios with a known bound on the variation budget and a non-bounded case. For MDPs with varying but bounded variation budgets, our bounds take the form $T^{1-k}k+1$, where $k$ is the variation budget per parameter. In cases with unbounded variation budgets, the bounds are $\tilde{O}(\log^{*}T)$. Furthermore, for Markov decision differential games (MDDGs), under both stationary and non-stational settings, we propose modification rules to ensure existence and uniqueness of value functions, thereby enabling the application of ALGO to MDDGs. For MDDGs with fixed but unknown variation budgets, we establish bounds of $T^{1-k}k+1$ for both dynamic risk and regret. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of average cost optimality equations (ACOEs) and coupled variational inequalities (CVIs) to MDDGs with non-stationary best response dynamics. Finally, numerical experiments on a simulated supply chain network demonstrate that ALGO effectively achieves high risk aversion in non-stationary environments, outperforming existing methods by over 50%. Overall, our experimental findings indicate that ALGO offers substantial improvements over prior approaches.

Such a continuous set of parameters is generally expected to prevent clear distinctiveness among low-lying string states, thereby hindering the formation of string resonant structures; consequently, analyzing explicit string-theoretic amplitumes becomes crucial for investigating this phenomenon. Our findings indicate that for relevant models, many details are governed by model-independent amplitude estimates, while specific features must be determined through explicit computations. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for extending amplitude calculations to lower-energy regimes, thereby enabling the study of vacuum selection mechanisms in these models.

(WIMPs) in compact objects like white dwarfs (WDs) accelerates them to the three-body Fermi surface. The energy of captured WIMPs typically matches the kinetic energy of colliding electrons. Assuming WIMP-nucleon interaction via vector or scalar coupling, the capture rate generally declines as local dark matter density decreases due to lower WIMP flux. However, in WDs with masses exceeding approximately $10^{23}$ grams ($M_\oplus$), the capture rate actually rises with decreasing local density. This counterintuitive behavior stems from reduced WIMP scattering angles resulting from smaller momentum transfer. Consequently, WIMPs retain higher energies after absorption in low-density environments. Since WIMP acceleration is most effective in the least dense WDs, the $\tau^{+} \tau^{-}$ annihilation channel within these stellar remnants could serve as an alternative source for positrons. We define the minimum WD mass where WIMP acceleration is viable as the "white dwarf ignition mass." For a 1 km radius WD, we estimate this threshold mass using muon-nucleus scattering as a proxy for WIMP-nucleus scattering. The vector or scalar nature of the coupling does not significantly alter this ignition mass estimate. Furthermore, the ignition mass proof holds true for nucleon-independent dark matter scattering. Any such dark matter with suitable mass and coupling constants could trigger extra energy sources in WDs formed at the ignition mass. Notably, the ignition mass is distinct from neutrino cooling thresholds; a vector-coupled dark matter with nucleon mass $\lesssim 10^{13}$ GeV could ignite a $10^{-7} M_\odot$ WD. A scalar-coupled dark matter with nucleon mass $\lesssim 10^{11}$ GeV could ignite a $10^{-6} M_\odot$ WD. A vector-coupled dark matter with nucleon mass $\lesssim 10^{10}$ GeV could ignite a $10^{-5} M_\odot$ WD. In contrast, an scalar-coupled dark matter with nucleon mass $\lesssim 10^{8}$ GeV could ignite a $10^{-4} M_\odot$ WD. We also provide general proofs that the ignition mass is independent of nucleon mass, nuclear structure factors, and electron number. Finally, we propose a novel vector dark matter model capable of igniting ultra-low mass white dwarfs.

Specifically, we show that both TVE and out-of-time-order correlation (OTOC) profiles converge to universal scaling forms that rely exclusively on parameters characterizing the circuit. Cross-domain recommendation addresses the challenge of enhancing prediction accuracy for weakly populated user-item bins by exploiting statistics from related domains. However, significant theoretical and practical hurdles remain, primarily concerning domain shift and data integration. While prior work has extensively addressed data integration, few studies have focused on domain alignment. Addressing this gap, we propose Cross-Domain Skill Learning via Adversarial Distribution Selection. This approach employs a domain selection network to identify similar users across domains and a domain adversarial network to align these identified groups, thereby ensuring that knowledge transfer occurs only between truly comparable user sets. We validate that this method effectively mitigates domain shift and substantially boosts recommendation performance. Experiments show consistent superior performance over baseline methods across various cold-start and sparse datasets. Historically, modeling efforts in economics and finance have been divided into two distinct camps: economic models, which utilize rationality and differential equations, and probabilistic models, which rely on stochastic processes. Despite their practical success, probabilistic models have faced criticism for failing to convey the intuitive understanding of a phenomenon. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, combining theory introduces significant challenges due to the complexity of hadronic cross sections. These sections depend on numerous inputs, including PDFs, fragmentations, parton-to-parton transition matrices, and renormalization and factorization scales. Although some procedures are straightforward to implement, others are difficult to understand or lack clear, unambiguous data interfaces. ### Fulltext:
Parameter seeding of a microresonator frequency comb (microcomb) typically depends on high continuous-wave (CW) input power. However, pulsed lasers can effectively excite CW microcombs by leveraging their dense comb mode structure and short pulse repetition periods. In this study, we used a single mode from a pulsed fiber laser to precisely position the mode frequencies of a Sealed Cavity Erbium-Doped Fiber Ring Microcomb (SCERFRIM) microcomb. By coaligning and coupling this isolated laser mode with two adjacent microcomb modes, we achieved mode synchronization between the pulselaser and the microcomb, resulting in the deterministic prediction of microcomb mode frequencies. This synchronization relies on the shared repetition rate of the pulse laser and the microcomb. Additionally, we showed that deterministic frequency prediction of microcombs is robust against mode coupling losses in the microresonator. Our results offer fresh perspectives on handling optical nonlinearities in microresonators, advancing applications in physical sciences, sensing, and optical communications. Furthermore, the inherent simplicity of our approach provides a new perspective on nonlinear dynamics in complex systems and a novel framework for fundamental nonlinear physics and control theory.

This area investigates two primary scenarios: first, where both the verifier and server are quantum capable; and second, where only the server possesses quantum capabilities, forcing the verifier to classically simulate the interaction. This paper enhances existing complexity bounds for various quantum verification protocols, particularly by allowing the verifier's resources to more closely match those of the circuit being validated. For a circuit characterized by $n$ qubits and $T$ gates, the findings establish the following complexities:

1. A quantum-verifier protocol requiring $n+T$ qubits and $T$ gates, achieving an exponential error decay of $\exp(-\Omega(T))$.
2. A quantum-verifier protocol requiring $n$ qubits and $T\cdot \text{poly}(\log(T))$ gates, yielding an error decay of $\exp(-\Omega(T)/\text{poly}(\log(T)))$.
3. A classical-verifier protocol needing $n\cdot \text{poly}(\log(n,T))$ qubits and $T$ gates, with an error decay of $\exp(-\Omega(\log(T)))$.
4. A classical-verifier protocol requiring $n$ qubits and $T^3$ gates, maintaining an error decay of $\exp(-\Omega(T))$.

Notably, the complexities listed in items 2 and 4 represent the first known improvements upon previous results, which were respectively $T$ and $T^4$. Furthermore, several new techniques are introduced and demonstrated to be broadly applicable, including methods for bounding the complexity of computing approximate unitaries, for analyzing computation within amplitude amplification frameworks, and one that enables the simulation of round-by-round interactions between a quantum client and server using offline interactions, provided the resources scale linearly with the number of rounds. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that any protocol complexity can be represented as a function of the circuit's depth rather than the count of its gates. This insight is crucial for conveying the efficiency of quantum verification in a manner consistent with standard complexity theory. This paper examines two prominent theories—internal models and optimal control—and highlights the fundamental conflict between them. The optimal control theory assumes the brain functions as a black box, inferring hidden control strategies from observable input-output data using external algorithms. Conversely, internal models posit that the brain anticipates its own outcomes by constructing internal models of its control mechanisms and their effects. By applying a unifying framework for multiple optimal control theories, we demonstrate that optimal strategies can be predicted solely from internal models. Specifically, we show that the internal model, optimal control policy, and observed behavioral data are mutually derivable. We contend that this synthesis of internal models and optimal control addresses the apparent paradox between these two prominent control theories. Furthermore, our findings suggest a resolution to the reverse control problem by demonstrating that optimal control policies can be learned internally, a capability that may be essential for the development of cognitive functions. Finally, we believe that a more profound reconciliation of internal models and optimal control theories is necessary to establish a comprehensive framework for neuroscientific control theory. By integrating internal models and optimal control, the resulting framework holds significant promise for advancing computational neuroscience. We look forward to the future exploration and discovery within this domain. This paper introduces SoundNet, a novel end-to-end convolutional neural network designed for this dual task. SoundNet is built upon a hierarchical source representation system, where successive layers encode increasingly higher-level abstracts of individual sound sources. This investigation represents the initial step in exploring auto-correlated effects using a physically motivated model; future work will examine other stochastic models and their specific impacts on remnant planetesimal disks and acoustical disk tracers.

This work investigates two notable cases of measurement-based feedback: spin-squeezing via continuous measurements and measurements with finite resolution. First, we analyze the case of continuous measurements with ideal readout, which is limited by dark counting noise. Gravity causes the larger, heavier disks to settle at the channel's ends, forming clusters, while the smaller, lighter ones remain dispersed throughout the bulk. While continuum modeling effectively predicts the size of these heavy disk clusters, it fails to accurately estimate the total number of disks within the lighter cluster. To address this, we introduce a novel hybrid modeling approach that integrates discrete modeling for the larger disks with a continuous approximation treating the smaller disks as a fluid. This hybrid method successfully predicts both the individual counts and the respective total numbers of each disk type within their formed clusters. Furthermore, this merging of discrete and fluid modeling techniques can be readily applied to other granular systems exhibiting phase separation, such as the grain size segregation observed during dry rolling over undulating topography. Furthermore, the hybrid model reveals a power-law scission between the total number of small disks and the count of large disks within the small disk cluster, thereby validating a recently proposed scaling law for gravitational clustering in alternating mixtures. Finally, a comprehensive comparison between hybrid and discrete-only models is made. Although both models yield similar results regarding cluster scission and overall phase separation, the hybrid model provides more detailed insights into the distribution of the smaller disks within the channel's central region. Additionally, by accounting for a broader range of physical parameters, the hybrid model enhances efficiency when detailed data on all components are required. These findings have potential applications in various fields, including ball bearings, granular coatings, and coated steel strands. Additionally, this work underscores the utility of combining discrete and fluid modeling approaches in granular research. Such a methodology could extend to other phenomena where smaller particles float amidst a collection of larger, settling grains.

By examining a specific experimental setup, we show that for absorbing materials (α > 1/d), the model predicts P ≥ 1, which contradicts physical reality. This process yields Acoustic Bow Shock Transients (ABOSTs), characterized by shock-driven supersonic winds that illuminate surrounding circumstellar matter (CSM). This study investigates ABOST interaction with CSM to establish observable signatures for identifying MBH direct collapse events. We analyze the light curve morphology, peak luminosity, and spectral characteristics of ABOSTs across various CSM structures, ultimately defining potential future observational markers. Under a standard CSM mass of $10^{3}$ M$_{\odot}$ and a typical MBH mass of 30 M$_{\odot}$, we recommend searching for high-luminosity peaks ($10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$) in the early post-starburst phase of stellar evolution. Observable redshifts range from $z$=0.01 to 0.1, with blackbody temperatures between 10,000 K and 30,000 K. If CSM is more massive ($10^{4}$ M$_{\odot}$), the peak luminosity increases by one order of magnitude, and the preferred redshift shifts to $z$<0.005 or $z$>0.05. Furthermore, ABOST peak brightness is highly sensitive to CSM structure; for instance, within a dense equatorial disk, the brightness is approximately 100 times greater than in a uniform distribution. These findings provide a theoretical basis for supporting the existence of MBH direct collapse events and offer guidance for identifying ABOST sources. Additionally, we detail future research directions regarding ABOST detection using specific CSM mass and structural parameters. Our conclusions assume a standard CSM composition of $X$=0.7 and $Z$=0.3. These insights contribute to understanding stellar evolution during the early universe and the formation of primordial black holes. Finally, this research offers a theoretical foundation for the design and operational strategies of upcoming astronomical observatories. Although flat bands have been identified in various two-dimensional materials, their presence in three-dimensional (3D) systems remains rare. This study demonstrates that multilayer black phosphorus exhibits multiple flat bands within a three-dimensional information valley flat band (IVFB) framework. Information valleys correspond to regions of negative curvature in the electronic band structure that generate effective flat bands upon accounting for local electron-electron interactions. By systematically analyzing black phosphorus's band structure, we reveal that these IVFBs arise from the interplay between 3D electron connectivity, strong spin-orbit coupling, and pronounced lattice anisotropy. Within these bands, the quasiparticle effective mass ranges from 3 to 5 times the electron mass, and electron-electron interactions are sufficiently strong to flaten the bands. Consequently, information valleys represent true flat bands resulting from many-body effects, rather than accidental single-particle flat bands. We propose that this III-VI group of black group 5 elements, characterized by inversion symmetry breaking and intrinsic layer coupling, offers a promising platform for exploring various correlation-induced quantum phenomena in 3D flat bands. Furthermore, information valleys may exist in other multi-layered systems where inversion symmetry is broken and layers are strongly coupled.

We propose employing deep learning to automatically generate high-fidelity annotations for genome assemblers, thereby reducing the need for a large volume of specialized annotation reads. Specifically, we introduce a convolutional neural network called ANN-Graph that learns to predict gene structures and other genomic features directly from raw sequence data. Our method is scalable, requiring only a limited set of genome reads during the training phase. Furthermore, ANN-Graph produces a confidence score for each predicted annotation, enabling the prioritization of high-fidelity results. This research establishes a novel approach to high-fidelity gene structure prediction grounded in deep learning and read-based analytics. By generating millions of top-fidelity annotations across all eukaryotic genomes, this deep learning framework has the potential to be widely adopted in genome assemblers. As a proof of concept, we applied these predicted gene structures to assist the MAUVE genome aligner. MAUVE utilizes a limited number of annotation reads to index gene structures, facilitating rapid and accurate alignment of gene structures and indels across genome Assemblies. We show that the highest-fidelity gene structures predicted by ANN-Graph can replace the annotation reads in MAUVE, resulting in substantial time and cost savings. Our findings indicate that this deep learning approach to gene structure prediction can enhance genome Assemblies, maintain a low reader count, and significantly reduce both expense and computational costs. Additionally, we have developed a Shiny application allowing users to input a gene of interest and a list of reads to explore the predicted gene structure, prediction confidence scores, and supporting reads. This publication and its associated software aim to advance deep learning applications in genomics and facilitate the adoption of this innovative, deep learning-driven approach to gene structure prediction.

Expanding on [MMMM15], we examine cut-elimination in multiplicative linear logic through the lens of algebraic geometry, extending the analysis to encompass multimolecular formulas. While much of our investigation remains limited to multiplicative logic, we introduce elimination graphs that illustrate the correspondence between cut-elimination steps in multimolecular proof structures and geometric operations such as blowing up and projecting within their associated varieties. Specifically, we examine stock price volatility and stock liquidity (measured by bid-ask spreads) in the months following major California wildfires using a difference-in-differences approach. (NLP) applications designed for code-mixed (CM) or multilingual text, driven by widespread user engagement across language boundaries in social media and online forums. However, creating effective NLP models for CM text has recently encountered a significant hurdle: data scarcity. This scarcity arises primarily from the labor-intensive and costly nature of manual data annotation and the restricted access to paid annotation services. Consequently, there is a growing demand for automated annotation techniques. While previous studies in automated annotation have focused heavily on optimizing model architectures, this often neglects fundamental issues related to how annotations are generated. Specifically, existing research has assumed that the quality of an annotation model is directly proportional to its complexity, leading to increasingly elaborate designs. In contrast, our research demonstrates that the true limiting factor is sufficient high-quality training data. Drawing on Caplan's Capacity Theory, we argue that text classification stands as a discriminative learning task with a well-defined optimal complexity determined by the training dataset. Furthermore, we illustrate that over-fitting is a pervasive issue in prior work and that adequate performance can be achieved with a relatively simple baseline model, provided the annotation process is fully automated. Empirical results across four text classification tasks in English, Hindi, Bengali, and Urdu confirm that simple annotation models outperform complex ones, often exceeding their performance by up to 10 points. Collectively, these findings indicate that the primary bottleneck in automated annotation lies not in model complexity, but in securing adequate high-quality training data. This insight offers a promising avenue for advancing automated annotation for text mixing and other challenging linguistic scenarios. Caplan's Capacity Theory, an information-theoretic framework, has been instrumental in revolutionizing various machine learning domains, including speech recognition, optical character recognition, and machine translation, for over three decades. Its core tenet asserts that an optimal task performance can be achieved with a model whose capacity is carefully aligned with the training data. Crucially, this optimal performance can be attained with a significantly simpler model, as the model's capacity is independent of the specific training examples. This report offers an overview of Caplan's Capacity Theory, highlighting its application to discriminative learning tasks, and elaborating on how it elucidates the role of training data. Caplan's Capacity Theory, which has revolutionized various machine learning domains over the past thirty years, serves as the foundation of this research. Its core argument is that the optimal performance on a discriminative learning task can be achieved with a model of carefully selected capacity, which is dictated solely by the high-quality training data. Fisher employed a complex argument grounded in calculus, which Fisher (1930, p. 41) described as "the most difficult part" of his work. Subsequent scholars, such as Cavalli-Sforza and Ford, found this justification opaque and deemed it invalid, prompting them to seek alternative proofs. This study establishes a rigorous proof of the Fundamental Theorem by leveraging basic linear algebra and by clearly distinguishing between the frequency-dependent fitness of genotypes and fitness independent of frequency, thereby fulfilling the theorem's requirements in its original form. Furthermore, we demonstrate the theorem using an elementary calculus approach. Although these methods lack the level of fine grain required to satisfy all conditions stipulated by Fisher, they effectively meet the demands of the theorem and may even exceed them. Finally, by contrasting Fisher's proof with the approaches of Cavalli-Sforza and Ford, we argue that his derivation is no more mathematically challenging than theirs and that it avoids the specific issues they introduced. Our analysis confirms that the difficulties Fisher encountered were no greater than those faced by later researchers, and we contend that clarifying the requirements of the Fundamental Theorem is essential for the proper teaching of population genetics. Above all, this work aims to render the justification for Fisher's most significant contribution to the field both rigorous and comprehensible. Above all else, Fisher's proof rests on a biological assumption that is distinctly non-mathematical.

We begin by reviewing the foundational concepts of feedback synthesis for closed-loop stabilization of pure states in MAME (methylamine) molecules, introducing two key Constrained State Reduction (CSR) algorithms that simplify state space representation by exploiting the commutativity of state transitions under control input applications. We apply these two CSR algorithms to build a MAME model for methylamine, illustrating how they facilitate the synthesis of feedback control for open-loop state stabilization. Specifically, we detail the design of a feedback controller capable of stabilizing the molecule in its ground state, $000b$. Additionally, we present experimental findings indicating that our synthesized feedback controller successfully steers methylamine from its ground state to a different target state. Experimental outcomes regarding transition probabilities, state lifetimes, total state preparation times, and similar metrics will be included in the full version of this technical report. Finally, we discuss potential enhancements for future feedback synthesis work, such as incorporating quantum effect operators into the CSR algorithms to further reduce the CSR graph of MAME. This research was conducted while the author was a summer intern at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences Quantum Algorithms and Architectures Summer School. Our technical work builds upon our preliminary findings, which can be found in arXiv:2105.01908v2.

Keywords: Quantum Control, Quantum Feedback, Quantum State Stabilization, MAME, Quantum Graph.

Quantum computing relies on precisely manipulating molecular states to perform computations. This process involves two main steps: first, preparing the molecular system in a target state, and second, executing a computation by applying time-dependent Hamiltonians to manipulate this state. While chemical synthesis is typically used for preparation, leveraging symmetries in molecular state transitions during computational manipulation can significantly lower the complexity of preparing target states. This paper introduces a approach to quantum state preparation that exploits these transition symmetries to efficiently generate target states.

Prior research indicates that for short-stay treatments, the length of service is a critical determinant of cost; however, determining the optimal duration has received little attention. Utilizing administrative data from Israel's largest teaching hospital, we examine how increasing treatment duration impacts patient health and cost within the ED. Our analysis reveals that while prolonged treatment increases costs, it does not consistently improve patient health. Specifically, the majority of patients do not require extended treatment to achieve their objectives. Additionally, we extended the Imputation by Ratios (IBR) method to manage multi-dimensional unobserved variables and address potential confounders. Through two simulation studies, we demonstrate that TSRI yields less biased estimates and achieves superior coverage rates compared to IBR, even in scenarios with perfectly exogenous treatment duration and no unobserved confounders. We validate these simulation insights using real-world data regarding patient time spent driving after alcohol consumption.

Consequently, academic research in this field has grown exponentially. Although significant progress has been made in developing path planning algorithms for autonomous navigation across various environments—including roads, campuses, and simulated virtual spaces—substantial efforts remain necessary before fully functional AVs can be deployed in real-world settings. This study examines interface conditions in various epitaxial growth methods applied to GaAs quantum dots, a material system widely utilized across quantum information initiatives. By combining low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and photoluminescence techniques, we investigate how different interface properties influence the optical properties of dots, specifically their optical transition energies. Specifically, we focus on the behavior of photino-maion mixing in the early universe during the transition from the symmetric phase to the broken phase. We demonstrate that, contrary to expectations, this mixing can remain non-vanishing at the transition point, leading to distinct consequences for the photino mass. Utilizing a path integral formulation, we apply the Ginzburg-Landau framework to examine the order of the phase transition and its impact on photino survival rates. Through the study of the order parameter and the associated scaling exponents, we establish the existence of a continuous (second-order) phase transition occurring at a critical temperature of $T_c=0$, which aligns with experimental photino constraints. Additionally, we derive the influence of the critical exponent $\beta$ on the phase transition and associated phenomena using the renormalization group approach. Finally, we explore the phase structure near the minimal SUSY point by analyzing the critical exponent $\nu$ for the correlation length and an additional exponent $\gamma$ via the bootstrap technique. Our findings indicate that the photino mass can be significantly altered by the order of the phase transition and relevant parameters near the minimal SUSY point. This scenario offers a promising solution to the photino survival problem, provided that $\nu$ and $\gamma$ can be derived from the bootstrap technique. These results enhance our understanding of the phase structure near the minimal SUSY point and suggest a viable strategy to address the photini survival issue. Finally, the derived critical exponents can be experimentally investigated using a setup involving an internal magnet and an evaporation chamber. We derive the finite-size grand canonical distribution, demonstrating that in the thermodynamic limit, it converges to a Poisson distribution characterized by a time-dependent mean profile and a constant variance. Our analytical findings are supported by numerical simulations. These results indicate that the time-averaged density derived from the finite-size distribution remains independent of system size and accurately represents the single-file density profile observed in simulations. Furthermore, we note that the fluctuations around the mean profile scale linearly with time, a phenomenon attributable to the focused nature of particle trajectories in one dimension. While the large-time asymptotic distribution for parallel-update TASEP remains an open problem, our findings provide fresh perspectives on this subject. In particular, we show that the finite-size grand canonical distribution follows universally solvable difference-differential equations, which may serve as a potential tool for addressing this open challenge. Our methodology is also extendable to more complex models involving multi-particle updates. Finally, we anticipate these theoretical developments to be applicable to other lattice models featuring multi-particle updates.

Fermi gases is predicted to occur in spin-imbalanced mixtures of alkali atoms when the scattering length between atoms of different spins diverges. We present a new theoretical framework for a dilute ferromagnetic gas incorporating magnetic field effects. Using the density matrix expansion (DME) method, we derive an effective nonlinear Schrödinger's equation from the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations coupled with the Maxwell equations. The stability analysis of this equation reveals magnetic domain wall modes and demonstrates ferromagnetic ordering stabilized by magnetic dipole interactions. Furthermore, we investigate the formation of ferromagnetic domains and calculate the radius of these domains using a variational approach. Our findings indicate that the domain radius is proportional to the s-wave scattering length enhanced by a factor determined by the dipole-polarizability, and it increases as the magnetic field intensity decreases. These results show qualitative agreement with recent experimental observations. Additionally, we examine the creation of droplets and the formation of supersolid tubes. We demonstrate that long-range phase coherence persists in the ferromagnetic domain and argue that magnetic dipole interactions enable the stabilization of supersolid tubes at values of the dimensionless dipole-potential energy for which dipolar supersolids are otherwise unstable. This represents the first proposal of a system where superfluidity exists without the protective mechanism of the Landau criterion. Finally, the existence of phase coherence within magnetic domains suggests potential applications in quantum simulation and the quantum storage of information. A detailed discussion of these applications is provided in the Appendix.

In machine learning, the most prevalent models are random-knowledge frameworks, which randomly assign knowledge or features to instances. Although this approach is widely adopted, its justification remains obscure. This paper presents a distinct probabilistic model for machine learning that focuses on the random-weight assumption: both instance representations and weights are treated as random variables. We derive the joint probability distribution for the lower half of the diagonal of the nonHermitian Hamiltonian, corresponding to a strongly localized near-edge state, and analyze its asymptotic behavior for large $N$. A semi-classical analysis of the Dyson map yields a joint probability distribution for $N$ nonHermitian eigenvalues, revealing that the edge behavior for strongly localized states mirrors that of a clean system with a magnetic field. Our study of the joint probability distribution for the diagonal elements of the Hamiltonian in a strongly localized near-edge state deepens our understanding of the classical conductance of quantum 2D disordered electrons. Wright's equation, serves as a fundamental mathematical model for population growth. Although it is relatively uncomplicated, it exhibits striking and unusual dynamics. This note aims to clarify some of these phenomena by employing basic techniques within frequency domain control theory. Specifically, we utilize the concept of characteristic exponent to investigate periodic solutions and relaxation oscillations. While this approach is typically reserved for linear systems, we demonstrate its efficacy for nonlinear problems by applying linearization and the Implicit Function Theorem. Notably, we establish that the delayed logistic equation can possess infinitely many periodic solutions and can approximate almost any smooth periodic orbit. Furthermore, we show that by selecting appropriate delays, the equation can generate periodic solutions with arbitrarily large amplitudes and periods. Our analysis also reveals that the role of delay in this equation is analogous to gain in linear frequency domain control theory. By leveraging insights from control theory, we prove that nearly every dynamic behavior observable in first-order linear systems with time delays also occurs in the delayed logistic equation. Finally, as an illustration of the accessibility of our method, we examine a well-known extension of the delayed logistic equation, which is widely regarded as the most notorious equation in mathematical biology. This model incorporates amplitude saturation at high frequencies, causing system output to diminish as input increases, thereby introducing nonlinearity in the frequency domain. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that many of the same analytical tools apply, allowing for the investigation of periodic solutions and relaxation oscillations within this more general framework. The primary distinction lies in the inability to utilize the Implicit Function Theorem, as the system lacks translational symmetry. Instead, we linearize within the frequency domain using a specialized variant of the Implicit Function Theorem designed for transcendental equations. This linear model includes a parameter of interest; by analyzing its dependence on delay, we derive a set of inequalities that determine the existence of periodic solutions and relaxation oscillations, consistent with prior research. Finally, we propose specific extensions to our periodic solutions and relaxation oscillations framework that could facilitate the analysis of a broad class of second-order nonlinear differential equations. This includes notable examples such as the van der Pol equation and the Duffing equation, both of which can be formulated as delayed logistic equations, and a simple delayed logistic model for competition between two species. By representing these systems in the frequency domain, we can determine if they can be cast as scalar delay-differential equations. If so, existing extensive literature on delayed logistic dynamics allows for the derivation of new insights into these previously challenging second-order nonlinear systems. In this study, we investigate two pathways to ideal engines: first, quantum systems functioning as hybrid machines capable of executing multiple useful tasks, and second, the reduction of fluctuations during these operations. For classical devices, the elimination of fluctuations requires high entropy production, as mandated by thermodynamic uncertainty relations. We extend these relations to multiterminal conductors operating as hybrid thermal machines. Our results demonstrate that quantum conductors surpass these classical limits, illustrated by a double quantum dot connected to normal metals and a reservoir that generates entangled Cooper pairs. This quantum reservoir drives the system into a correlated steady state, enabling the device to deliver both electric and heat currents with fluctuations that are either suppressed or amplified. Consequently, this system achieves a coefficient of fluctuation exceeding that of a classical analog by more than two orders of magnitude, thereby realizing a hybrid machine with optimal dual functionality. Furthermore, entropy production in this system adheres to classical-like uncertainty relations. Finally, we examine conductance fluctuations in quantum devices and report their experimental observation. The dual benefits of quantum technologies include enhanced efficiency and the ability to control fluctuations in multi-terminal conductors.

Experimental observation of the quantum uncertainty principle remains a significant challenge. While quantum fluctuations are inherent to these principles, directly measuring them is difficult due to measurement backaction. Consequently, prior research has relied on calculating measurable consequences, such as correlations between quantum operators, uncertainty products, variance products, and covariance matrices. However, these approaches often lack direct physical interpretation, are challenging to measure, or require extensive data collection. To address this, we propose a novel detector capable of simultaneously observing entropy and observables with minimal disturbance, thereby directly accessing information content. Using this quantum detector, we operationalize the uncertainty principle for quantum states. Through numerical simulations, we apply this method to various scenarios, confirming its general applicability. We also investigate related concepts, such as the thermodynamic uncertainty relation, which is often difficult to operationalize. We demonstrate that our method can measure correlations between measured operators and the detector's internal degrees of freedom, allowing for the direct assessment of information content, uncertainty, and the backaction of weak measurements. We conclude that this method offers a new, straightforward pathway to experimentally access the uncertainty principle. This letter was developed in collaboration with S. Gupt and C. M. This study examines how public sector officials evaluate their reliance on Google, their awareness of potential biases arising from personalized search, and the feasibility of disabling this feature to enhance reliability during critical decisions. Question 1: What drives the need for reduction?

Answer 1: A primary rationale is the substantial gap—spanning three to four orders of magnitude—between the computational resources required by current climate models and those needed to meet future requirements, without necessarily compromising efficiency, accuracy, or software robustness. Simplification offers a pathway to bridge this gap.

Beyond this primary driver, other reasons include:
*   **Scientific insight**: Reduction often yields key qualitative insights that are inaccessible through other methods.
*   **Validation and verification**: It facilitates the comparison and validation/verification of models at different scales.
*   **Model component reduction**: These techniques are also applicable to individual model components, such as cloud parameterizations.
*   Proper scaling and normalization are essential to interpret numerical results meaningfully.

Question 2: What are the primary categories of model reduction techniques?

Answer 2: Methods are generally classified into two broad categories: those providing control over the reduced model's structure and those that do not. Within the first category, we distinguish between:
*   **Structure-preserving methods**: These retain the fundamental properties of the original system, such as conservation laws or specific model structures.
*   **Generic projection methods**: These rely on selecting subspaces based on physical insights or statistical analysis of snapshots, often resulting in reduced models with altered structures.

A second classification organizes methods based on the level of control they offer over the reduced model:
*   **Nonmodal reduction**: Typically produces reduced models of arbitrary structure, though some modal methods can be adapted nonmodally.
*   **Modal reduction**: Generally yields reduced models with a structured, often orthogonal basis.

Finally, reductions are classified by the extent to which they provide control over the original model:
*   **Discrete reductions**: Focus on reducing large discrete systems.
*   **Continuous extensions**: These techniques are primarily developed for continuous PDEs but are increasingly applicable to discrete models, particularly in earth-system contexts.

Across all categories, it is crucial to rigorously quantify both approximation accuracy and computational efficiency.

Among the various astronomical instruments deployed to search for electromagnetic counterparts, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) played a critical role by conducting rapid observations of the sky surrounding the merger site. Leveraging HST's unique capability to obtain deep near-ultraviolet and optical imaging alongside precise astrometry, these observations significantly advanced our understanding of the merger's electromagnetic signature and the associated kilonuminous transient. Furthermore, the data collected by HST is essential for constraining the equation of state for nuclear matter. This review summarizes the scientific outcomes derived from the electromagnetic data obtained by HST and other telescopes. Specifically, we demonstrate how photometry from the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) and the Advanced Camera for Survey (ACIS) enabled the measurement of the transient's total mass energy budget and the determination of its total projected mass. Additionally, HST's contributions to the study of r-process nucleosynthesis are discussed. The site of gravitational wave emission was located with an elliptical error region of approximately 6 arcminutes by utilizing the electromagnetic counterpart seen by HST, along with data from ANTARES, VLT/GRAVITY, and Zwicky Transient Facility. Finally, we outline the scientific potential of future HST observations. With its large field of view and multi-epoch imaging of the error region, a future HST visit could enable the re-localization of the merger site elliptical region by a factor of 10 to 100, thereby constraining the electromagnetic origin of the kilonova and the neutron star equation of state. Such observations would complement archival data and support the planning of observations for other surveys and future observatories. Ground-based spectrographs employ various instruments to track star positions, a process known as astrometry, to position spectral lines accurately. These systems are susceptible to position variations caused by thermal expansion of mechanical components. While the precision of astrometry systems has improved in recent years, the resulting astrometric errors have been assumed to have a negligible impact on exoplanet detection. However, within a sample of 309 stars from the CORALIE/HARPS archive (1999–2012), we identified ten high-signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) residuals, exceeding 100 times the root mean square (RMS) of the data. These residuals suggest a variability with a 1-year period and an amplitude of at least 1 cm/s. This study presents the first evidence of a periodic ground-based astrometric signal, a phenomenon that has not been previously reported. This discovery underscores the necessity of continuously and rigorously monitoring astrometry system positions. Ground-based observations of exoplanets often face challenges from activity-induced stellar signals, particularly in detecting small planets with only a few high-precision measurements. We analyzed all available CORALIE data for known exoplanets, finding evidence of activity-induced variations in six systems with a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 10. This marks the first detection of such variations in the sample, with five cases likely due to stellar spots and one attributed to planetary magnetism

However, the true prevalence of these RL AGNs remains uncertain due to incomplete catalogues, biased flux limits, and incomplete luminosity function measurements. We utilized 12.5 million sources from the Catalina Real-time Transient Survey (Catalina-RTS) to measure the AGN luminosity function (LF) within 1 Mpc of clusters. Furthermore, searches for lepton-flavour-violating decays of neutral B mesons, such as $B^0 \to \mu^\pm e^\mp$, have yielded significant findings. Beyond the Standard Model, new sources of CP violation in neutral meson decays have been explored, including those from the Little Higgs with Extra $U(1)$ symmetries (LHT) model and the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM). In LHT, additional CP violation arises from non-trivial phases in the 3-2-2 gauge group and from non-perturbative effects in the strong sector. Conversely, in MSSM, new CP-violating phases emerge from the soft supersymmetry-breaking terms and the $\mu$ term. Given the extensive experimental evidence regarding CP violation in neutral meson decays, this work examines how such new CP-violating contributions manifest in these decays.

Climate change is an existential threat to humanity, a fact acknowledged by the vast majority of scientists. However, significant segments of the population remain skeptical or in denial, a phenomenon known as climate change misperception. This attitude, supported by scientific research, hinders efforts to combat the crisis. This paper examines the predictors of such misperceptions using representative survey data from eight countries collected between 2008 and 2016. Employing logistic regression analysis, the study identified individual-level factors that explain why some people reject the scientific consensus. Key predictors include perceived control over climate change, behavioral attitudes, and political party membership. Because trust in scientific institutions is itself predicted by perceived control and attitudes toward climate change, efforts to increase trust are limited by these prior beliefs. Consequently, the paper proposes a two-stage strategy: first, fostering trust in relevant institutions, and second, promoting awareness of the risks and the need for climate change prevention. The study underscores that perceived control acts as a critical barrier to both recognizing the problem and taking action, making trust in institutions capable of mitigating the crisis a vital prerequisite for meaningful engagement. These insights have profound implications for behavioral change initiatives and should guide future outreach and education programs. To overcome this, we require information extraction techniques capable of handling variations in expression, medical terminology, and implicit relationships. We introduce a new task called Symbolic Relation Extraction (SRE), designed to identify symbolic relationships between symptom terms and other words (e.g., "Headache is common"), which convey vital clinical insights. To train for SRE, we annotated a dataset covering diverse wording variations and implicit relationships in MEDICINE-UMLS-Annotated (MUMU), a new medical micro-domain of the MUMU-2.0 corpus. However, its application to high-stakes domains like nuclear fusion remains an emerging field, limited by a scarcity of cases. This study examines the specifics and results of case 1, which involved learning an operating point for the Advanced Toroidal Fusion Test Reactor (ATFT) using deep RL. In this first instance of applying reinforcement learning to advanced nuclear fusion, the primary challenge involved managing multiple constraints while maximizing output. To address this, we developed an observation space incorporating predictions for key variables, trained the agent with a reward function that prioritized power maximization and constraint compliance, and expanded the action space to incorporate physical knowledge. The resulting learned policy successfully identified operating points that maximized input power and adhered to all limits across various initial conditions. Notably, the power-maximizing point achieved values exceeding those of two predefined baseline policies in approximately 80% of initial condition distributions. Although this first application of deep RL to nuclear fusion yielded sub-optimal points compared to manually designed baselines in roughly 20% of initial conditions, the method remains viable for discovering superior points under more complex constraints. While generalization to other devices requires additional data, the success of this initial attempt demonstrates the potential of deep RL for significant advancements in nuclear fusion research. Beyond fusion, this approach is applicable to other advanced data-driven systems. Currently, we are extending these techniques to discover more efficient point scenarios for JET, one of the most advanced fusion experiments globally. Additionally, we intend to utilize this method for knowledge distillation, aiming to create compact neural network policies with reduced computational demands while maintaining performance comparable to the deep RL agent. These efforts will facilitate more practical and real-time applications of this methodology.

In this digital era, individuals not only consume information but also actively generate and share it through various online social media channels. These platforms facilitate two-way interactions that stimulate community engagement. Specifically, during crises, personal electronic devices enable rapid data collection and dissemination, while communication services foster connections that mobilize communities and inspire collective action. This research investigates the role of personal electronic devices in scientific literacy development by analyzing discussions on Wikipedia during the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, the impact of user-generated content is evaluated by counting FAQ sections and assessing their quality via inter-language entropy. Results indicate that Wikipedia experienced significantly higher usage and richer discourse regarding COVID-19 compared to other viral topics. The platform allowed users to access official information instantly and easily, leading to enriched interactions that went beyond mere information consumption. This was evidenced by a higher prevalence of FAQ sections in Chinese, Korean, and Japanese versions, demonstrating that Wikipedia can effectively scientific literacy by allowing users to actively participate in the flow of critical information. Ultimately, this capability highlights the potential value of personal electronic devices in enhancing public awareness and resilience.

However, the exchange of these parameters creates a vulnerability to membership inference attacks, which aim to determine if a specific individual's data was included in a participant's local dataset. This paper introduces a novel attack framework capable of reconstructing membership information across all participating clients in a federated learning system. By utilizing gradient reversal adversarial training (GRAD), which redirects gradient updates to adversarially perturb models, GRAD facilitates the theft of membership data while remaining undetectable to untrusted participants who remain within a trusted framework. To mitigate this threat, the paper proposes two countermeasures: (1) integrating an obfuscation layer into each participant's model, inspired by federated graph neural networks, and (2) employing differential privacy during aggregation to prevent any single party's information from being reconstructed. Empirical results confirm the practicality of both the attack and defense strategies. Notably, when applying differential privacy to synthesized gradients, an epsilon value below 3.0 successfully thwarts attacks while incurring a minimal accuracy loss of less than 0.5%. Overall, these findings aim to enhance the security understanding of federated learning systems for both contributors and providers.

Modern embedded devices offer extensive customization options through thousands of available libraries and modules; however, these choices significantly influence runtime performance. Consequently, executing and evaluating multiple configurations is essential for developing efficient systems. While traditional configuration management tools are designed for enterprise software, they are ill-suited for embedded contexts where runtime constraints must be considered. This paper introduces METIS, a framework designed to manage, emulate, and compare various library-based configurations alongside their runtime limitations. We demonstrate METIS using it as a case study for configurable real-time operating systems (RTOS). By selecting appropriate libraries and modules, developers can tailor an RTOS to specific requirements; for instance, disabling unnecessary network protocols reduces both software size and potential interrupt distractions. The study also examines runtime factors, such as knowing which tasks are critical for scheduling. We present meaningful findings regarding configurable real-time operating systems and provide guidance for future work. Additionally, we illustrate how METIS applies beyond RTOS configuration, offering a comprehensive example set. METIS is accessible via www.nicolas-heras.fr/metis/.

creating low-dimensional, low-distortion representations of intricate data structures. This work investigates embedding products of hyperbolic spaces $\mathbb H^2$ with Euclidean space $\mathbb R^h$. We demonstrate that for sufficiently large $h$, any graph $G=(V,E)$ can be embedded into $\mathbb H^2 \times \mathbb R^h$ while preserving adjacency. Specifically, vertices $u$ and $v$ are positioned at distance $\delta$ if and only if $u=v$ or $\{u,v\}\in E$. The proof relies on established results concerning hyperbolic embeddings of graphs. Furthermore, we show that achieving this precise reconstruction is impossible with a bounded distortion in $\mathbb H^2$ alone. As additional contributions, we derive hyperbolic embedding theorems for products of Euclidean spaces and for products of hyperbolic spaces under specific conditions. Finally, we apply these findings to highlight inherent limitations of various hyperbolic graph representation approaches. Together, these results suggest exploring the distortion-vs.-dimension tradeoff differently within hyperbolic geometry than is currently common. However, many open questions remain, including whether a similar embedding is feasible for $\mathbb H^2 \times \mathbb R^1$ and how to extend these methods to other curved spaces. Ultimately, hyperbolic geometry embeddings serve naturalists by enabling the recovery of an organism's ancestral environment from its genetic data.

This paper focuses on extending recent advances in compressive regression to various learning scenarios, offering refined theoretical guarantees and more practical algorithmic solutions. Specifically, we address regularized regression, deep network training, and model selection. Of particular significance is our demonstration that regularized regression can be solved with higher compression ratios and improved theoretical performance compared to prior compressed learning approaches. Furthermore, we show that deep network training is feasible without substantially altering the training process; rather, it can be achieved by training multiple models and selecting the optimal feature representation. This strategy yields promising results for deep learning, achieving high compression ratios with superior performance relative to existing learning-based compression methods. Finally, our approach to feature selection offers a novel perspective on the intersection of compressed learning and model selection, where models are chosen based on feature importance rather than solely on dataset size constraints. Collectively, these contributions establish a robust framework for measuring, analyzing, and synthesizing diverse compressive learning problems. The paper concludes with an outlook on future research directions at the intersection of compressed learning and statistical modeling. Supplementary materials accompanying this work include proven results and algorithms.

In this framework, when an agent shifts opinions, there is a noise-induced probability that the reverse transition also occurs; however, this probability differs for the two distinct values, resulting in asymmetry. This asymmetry parameter, denoted as $\alpha$, can be constant or dynamic, potentially dependent on the number of agents or their configuration. Our findings indicate that noise invariably drives the system toward parity, demonstrating that asymmetry is inherently non-generic within the broader context of voter models. Furthermore, we illustrate a scenario where a decrease in noise actually accelerates global consensus. We argue this happens because noise hinders the system from reaching a perfectly symmetric state, thereby masking the true consensus. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for opinion-based systems, such as social networks, emphasizing that asymmetry should not be viewed in isolation but as a property relative to a specific model class. Consequently, the voter model class represents a critical boundary case where agents exhibit a tendency toward equality rather than inequality.

While numerous defense mechanisms have been suggested, robust and systematic analysis of AEs has often been overlooked. This paper offers a rigorous examination of adversarial samples by integrating psychological and physical frameworks. We categorize AEs into two distinct types: Type-I AEs, which induce classification errors through subtle, nearly imperceptible perturbations, and Type-II AE outputs, which require obvious alterations to achieve misclassification. Our methodology employs techniques from physics and information theory to quantify adversarial samples, identifying their nature, characteristics, and associated costs. Specifically, we utilize Average Hamming Distance to measure Type-I AEs and the minimum number of pixel changes in binary images required for incorrect classification. Furthermore, we apply Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance to assess visual differences between original images and Type-II AEs within color channels. Applied to the MNIST dataset, our quantitative analysis demonstrates that AEs operate within well-defined boundaries. This enables reliable evaluation and comparison of existing defense strategies, fostering more robust and effective adversarial training. Notably, our analysis reveals that AEs possess inherent structure rather than randomness, suggesting that systematic countermeasures can be designed to neutralize these structured attacks. Ultimately, this work advances the scientific understanding of AEs and establishes a framework for developing robust defenses.

This study investigates the evolutionary paths of pre-main-sequence (PMS) stars by utilizing state-of-the-art stellar evolution models that incorporate both accretion and mass loss, alongside observational data on embedded stellar populations. We examined various evolutionary trajectories under different initial masses, ages, radii, and accretion and mass loss rate profiles to determine their impact on the star's trajectory within the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Our findings indicate that low-mass PMS stars evolve into more luminous objects through rapid accretion followed by quenching, exhibiting characteristics of the question posed earlier. Conversely, very massive PMS stars appear to form directly as luminous stars, with their evolution primarily driven by contraction toward the main sequence rather than accretion. We further explore whether the transformation from late-type to early-type stars occurs via direct formation or through evolutionary mechanisms involving accretion, mass loss, and interaction with circumstellar material. By analyzing specific evolutionary paths, we demonstrate that rapid accretion followed by quenching and mass loss can explain the observed shift from late-type to early-type stars in evolutionary tracks. These modeled PMS stars exhibit higher radii and lower surface temperatures than main-sequence stars of equivalent mass, suggesting a role for accretion in this transformation. This model aligns with evidence indicating angular momentum gain during accretion causes PMS stars to expand. However, the IEEE 802.11p standard provides an inadequate number of pilots for precise channel tracking, particularly in fast-moving vehicle environments where frequent channel mismatches between pilots can result in erroneous estimates and increased outage probabilities. Although traditional estimators such as the minimum mean square error (MMSE) and least-squares (LS) estimators are computationally efficient, their performance degrades under low pilot counts. This paper introduces a new Bayesian estimator named the subspace Bayesian estimator (SBE), which achieves reliable tracking with minimal pilots without the need for training. The SBE operates by reducing the search space for unknown parameters; specifically, it enhances MMSE estimates by incorporating the subspace structure derived from pilot positions. Since the SBE relies solely on statistical properties of the channel, it eliminates the need for training. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for its computational complexity. Simulation results demonstrate that SBE significantly outperforms conventional MMSE and LS estimators, achieving an approximate 40% reduction in outage probability compared to the standard MMSE estimator. Additionally, the proposed method incurs negligible computational cost, approximately 5% higher than LS. Although developed for IEEE 802.11p systems, the underlying methodology is applicable to other wireless technologies. Ultimately, the SBE is poised to enhance the performance of VANETs. Prior theoretical and experimental investigations have identified these waves in microwave and terahertz frequency ranges, demonstrating their emergence through a symmetric resistance transition from negative to positive values combined with uniform surface reactance. These waves exhibit self-localization resistance-imaginary reactance immittance singularities at the mid-point of this transition. In this study, we theoretically predict and experimentally verify the existence of line waves in microwave systems utilizing spatially modulated surface conductance that breaks mirror symmetry, specifically through a resistive surface combined with a uniform capacitive reactance. We demonstrate that line waves can be imagined to originate from capacitance singularities in regions where the surface resistance is negative. Furthermore, we show that line waves can be envisioned to arise at capacitance divergences in regions where the surface resistance is negative. These findings expand the design flexibility for line wave protocols and suggest new approaches for achieving wave self-localization. The surface conductance transition examined here represents the first nonreciprocal modulation ever examined for line wave emergence. Wave confinement mechanisms are shown to remain robust even when significant nonreciprocity causes a substantial redshift in the terahertz resonance. Finally, line waves are experimentally observed in capacitive-reactive microwave structures featuring either random or sawtooth surface conductance modulation. Across all configurations, line waves are detected via sharp terahertz surface peaks, with mode positions accurately predicted by the protocol. This mode localization is demonstrated in planar waveguides approximately one wavelength wide, confirming that terahertz line waves remain tightly confined to the surface edge despite having free-space wavelengths that would classically prohibit such confinement. We contend that these results broaden the design palette for line wave protocols, offering new avenues for future research, and suggest that self-localization may originate from entirely new classes of singularities in surface electrodynamics. Furthermore, we illustrate how to leverage line waves to create surface sensors and discuss how their exceptional localization and spectral characteristics enable the encoding of terahertz information along a two-dimensional spatial path. We conclude by suggesting how line waves facilitate access to hidden spectral information governed by spectral holography, marking an entirely new avenue for metasurface-inspired imaging techniques. Overall, we demonstrate that line waves represent a versatile class of emergent terahertz phenomena capable of enabling advanced functional innovations. We illustrate how they can serve as foundational components for metasurfaces exhibiting surface terahertz gyrational effects and as functional building blocks for various enhanced sensing protocols.

While recent self-supervised learning methods have leveraged forward-backward loss-rejection sampling to pretrain transformers, a rigorous theoretical analysis of rejection sampling remains absent. This work initiates probabilistic analysis by modeling the loss distribution as a discrete random variable. We derive the exact expected sample count after rejection sampling and prove that the variance of this count reaches its maximum precisely when every loss value appears with equal frequency. This phenomenon arises because noisy losses tend to cluster around specific values more intensely than clean losses. Based on these theoretical insights, we introduce a variational approach to minimize variance by post-processing the knowledge graph and filtering out samples with anomalously high losses. Empirical results demonstrate that this method significantly improves link prediction performance. Finally, we apply proposed techniques to real-world knowledge graphs, achieving substantial significant gains in micro-F1 scores.

In contrast, the time-splitting spectral method (TSSP) is a widely used, robust, and efficient numerical technique for NLSE solutions that is generally applicable even in the absence of a cubic term. While standard curvilinear manipulation techniques yield momentum operators that are Hermitian only in the absence of Christoffel symbols—which represent pseudo-Riemannian manifolds with non-vanishing Ricci tensors—valid quantum mechanics on such spaces necessitates a different approach. By demanding that momentum operators remain form form-preserving under coordinate transformations, we derive explicit expressions for them on manifolds with constant curvature. This capability enables the quantization of systems possessing both intrinsic and extrinsic curvature. We illustrate this application by determining the wavefunctions and eigenvalue equations for a particle confined to two-dimensional curved manifolds embedded in three-dimensional Minkowski space. Furthermore, we extend our formalism to systems exhibiting spin degrees of freedom by constructing the spin-momentum operator and applying it to a particle traveling along a de Sitter universe hypersurface. Finally, our methodology can be extended to arbitrary curved manifolds by incorporating curvature-dependent terms into the momentum operator; in this context, these terms represent quantum fields interacting with the curved manifold's curvature. This approach holds broad relevance for quantum field theory on curved manifolds, as it establishes the specific form of momentum operators and identifies their associated quantum fields. Additionally, our derived momentum operators can be integrated with spinors and other quantum fields to construct geometric algebra-based formulations for systems on curved manifolds. This represents a significant advancement, given that reliable methods for obtaining exact solutions to differential equations on curved manifolds are currently scarce. By utilizing curvature-dependent terms within the momentum operator, we enable the derivation of exact analytical solutions for various systems. We demonstrate this by solving the Dirac equation for extrinsically curved manifolds, illustrating how our formalism facilitates the acquisition of exact solutions. Incorporating curvature-dependent terms into the momentum operator allows for the determination of spinor wavefunctions and eigenvalues, thereby providing a viable alternative to the approximation methods typically required. This is particularly pertinent given the complexity of differential manifold structures, which often hinder the derivation of exact solutions. The utilization of curvature-dependent terms in the momentum operator offers a practical and exact approach to addressing the challenges inherent in solving differential equations on curved manifolds. Thus, this research provides a comprehensive and effective methodology for addressing the difficulties associated with differential equations on curved manifolds. We anticipate that our findings will serve as a foundational framework for investigating degrees of freedom on curved manifolds within the context of quantum gravity. This is especially significant given the current lack of a consistent theory of quantum gravity, a deficit often attributed to the complexity of differential manifold structures. This symmetry enables an alternative method for generating the characteristic operator necessary for composite Higgs models, operator 4 in our specific setup. Analysts typically discard this contribution under the assumption that Wilson coefficients for such terms are negligible. However, our findings indicate that these coefficients can be substantial, rendering the new term competitive with the leading ones. Consequently, the Higgs mass emerges as heavier, potentially resolving the little hierarchy problem, albeit at the expense of pushing the scale of the composite sector lower. A global fit incorporating LHC and LHCb constraints yields a precise prediction for the heavy Higgs mass of $M_{H^{\pm}}=300^{+180}_{-110}$ TeV. This $W'^{+}$ generates a distinctive signature producing a top quark and a heavy charged lepton (muon or tau), along with distinct signatures in Higgs and vector boson fusion channels. We conclude that even with remaining theoretical uncertainties, this model offers a promising prospect for the upcoming LHC run.

This study investigates how physically displacing a object post-pinchining alters human perception. Using a VR setup, we placed real-world objects at two distinct depths between the thumb and index finger. The participants' task was to estimate the physical separation between these two virtual positions. Our findings reveal that visually perceiving the object at two distinct locations significantly enhances the pinching effect, even for heavy items that are physically impossible to support at two levels simultaneously. Furthermore, the magnitude of this dual-pinch effect correlates with the actual distance between the two rendered positions. These results demonstrate that visual disambiguating the object's true location amplifies the pinching illusion, offering new insights into the mechanisms driving heavy object pinching.
