This study examines the elements influencing the model's language adaptability and analyzes the trade-offs between computational expenses and anticipated performance. Our results demonstrate that it is feasible to expand the model's language coverage with substantial performance gains without any additional training costs, provided the new languages belong to families for which the model already exhibits strong comprehension. Specifically, by leveraging existing language resources, we successfully increased the model's supported languages by 50% with negligible cost, achieving competitive performance on nearly all standard single- and multi-lingual benchmarks. Furthermore, we introduced new evaluation metrics and datasets to enhance the assessment of low-resource languages, both in monolingual and multilingual contexts. To facilitate this increased language coverage, we released a version of the model supporting 20 languages, which can be utilized for inference without any trivial additional financial burden. Our code repository also includes analysis tools designed to address critical questions regarding the factors that govern a model's language coverage. The release is accessible at https://philschuman.github.io/m-merlot-v2-en/. We anticipate that this work will inspire researchers to focus on understanding the variables controlling language adaptability in pretrained models, thereby enabling the cost-effective incorporation of new languages. Additionally, we aim to promote further research on pretrained models in under-resourced and historically marginalized languages. Our comprehensive suite of analyses and datasets offers a robust foundation for these efforts. The source code is available at https://github.com/philschuman/m-mernet-v2 and pending review by arXiv at https://arxiv.com/23/02/18217. All experiments were executed on an AWS instance equipped with a single p3.8xlarge GPU. While this choice incurs costs, the total expenditure remains trivial compared to the price of the pretrained model. We also paged through the AWS console and queried their support pages to verify language support. For low-resource languages, scores were calculated using ROUGE and similar metrics. Our analysis reveals several key insights: (1) language performance in M-MERLOT scales approximately logarithmically with language-specific data; (2) language families and neighboring languages benefit from shared parameters, allowing the model to pick up new languages with minimal Trained Parameters (MTPs); and (3) significant performance improvements can be achieved without retraining by utilizing in-domain data. We also highlight that our analysis of control variables offers actionable guidance for future language support.

When such a cover exists, the covering number $\sigma(R)$ denotes the cardinality of a minimal cover. A ring $R$ is defined as $\sigma$-elementary if $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for every nonzero two-sided ideal $I$. This paper presents the first instances of $\sigma$-elementary rings $R$ possessing a nontrivial Jacobson radical $J$ such that the quotient $R/J$ is noncommutative, and it establishes the covering numbers for these rings. Furthermore, the study derives an upper bound for $\sigma(R)$ applicable to all $\sigma$-elementary rings. The findings extend to the scenario where the subrings in the cover are not required to be subrings in the strict sense, provided that for each $a \in R$, the principal ideal $aR$ is contained in at most one member of the cover. Additionally, it is demonstrated that $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ holds for every nonzero two-sided ideal $I$ under these conditions as well. The results generalize to ring families where every principal two-sided ideal is contained in at most a specified number of cover members. However, the assumption that the cover has finite cardinality is essential for all primary results. Finally, the question of whether $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ necessarily holds when $R/J$ has a smaller covering number than $R$ is identified as the central open problem in this area.

Question Answering (QA) over news articles is a challenging task because it necessitates navigating varied document structures and executing complex reasoning to address questions. Current state-of-the-art QA systems rely on attention-based neural networks that process entire documents at once; however, this holistic approach fails to capture the local linguistic cues essential for solving many QA instances. This paper introduces a novel method that combines Linguistic Document Structure (LDS) features with state-of-the-art deep learning techniques to resolve these limitations. We extract features based on document sections and employ transition matrices to model inter-dependencies between them, effectively capturing structure granularity that uniform token-level processing overlooks. Our experiments demonstrate that these linguistic features, when integrated with deep learning methods, set a new state-of-the-art in QA performance. Additionally, we show that faking LDS does not degrade performance, but reconstructing only partial document structures significantly boosts results. These findings validate that our approach is robust to adversarial attacks while highlighting the critical role of linguistic structure in QA. To our knowledge, this is the first work to model document structure using transition matrices, offering a flexible and efficient solution for processing coarse-grained document units. We believe our results will inspire further research into applying linguistic and other structural knowledge to solve challenging tasks. Source code is available at https://github.com/aryehsh/linguistic-QA.

Comprehensive experiments on SSTM demonstrate significant performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines, with speed-ups reaching up to an order of magnitude faster than traditional graph query approaches. These results confirm that SSTTM effectively exploits both user relationships and discussion thread connectivity to achieve high performance. The code is accessible at https://github.com/byu-nlp/SSTM.

Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a potential for further exploration. To address this issue, we investigate loss functions within the context of tabular data using a systematic framework that categorizes losses into three groups based on their suitability for this domain. Our methodology evaluates a broad spectrum of loss functions by adapting existing benchmarks for tabular classification and regression, while also introducing a new, larger tabular classification task derived from the popular LibCVM dataset. In empirical studies, we examine how different loss functions perform when paired with tabular models, including Decision Trees, Gradient Boosted Trees, Gradient Boosted Neural Networks, MLP-PKDT, and Attention-PKDT. Our findings indicate that a group of "general" loss functions often outperforms other candidates, validating the previously observed success of cross-entropy in tabular classification. Additionally, we demonstrate that by integrating tabular information into transformer-based neural networks, we can effectively mitigate the sensitivity to loss function selection, enabling the use of group mean squared error—a loss function typically associated with computer vision. Finally, our results reveal that certain loss functions can yield models with lower test-time error, even when training-time error is comparable or inferior. Furthermore, we propose a selection method based on tabular data statistics that selects optimal loss functions with mean performance matching or surpassing that of fine-tuned hyperparameters. This work promotes a more rigorous evaluation of loss functions in tabular deep learning, fostering future research in this area. At each subsequent step, an index $i$ is chosen uniformly and randomly. If $i$ resides in a partition of size $k > 1$, it is moved to a new partition of size $k+1$ with a stochastic probability of 0 or 1; otherwise, the partitions remain unchanged. This mechanism generates two distinct processes, F-UT and F-DT, which correspond to the Facilitated Unimodal Transposition and Facilitated Descending Transfer processes, respectively. These are facilitation-based analogs of the well-established Top-Tabled Sort and Fast-Tabled Sort algorithms, differing primarily in their random index selection.

Both F-UT and F-DT begin with every element in its own partition and aim to reach a configuration where all elements are grouped into a single partition. Consequently, the primary performance metric is the mixing time, which for both processes is demonstrated to be $\Theta(n \log^2 n)$.

Beyond the mixing time, the facilitation-based nature of both processes induces inherent ordering within the partitions and their elements. Specifically, all elements within any given partition are consecutive integers, and the partitions themselves are ordered such that every element in partition $i$ is smaller than every element in partition $j$ where $i < j$. This structural property allows for the analysis of "slice processes," which focus exclusively on a specific partition. For both F-UT and F-DT, the mixing time of these slice processes is also proven to be $\Theta(n \log^2 n)$.

Furthermore, we establish that for both processes, the variance of the random partition size follows a log-quadratic distribution, i.e., $cn \log^2 n + O(\log n)$, and provide a detailed asymptotic distribution for this size. Finally, we examine several other variations of these processes, demonstrating that they share the same log-quadratic variance characteristics for final partition sizes. These include reinforced partitioning processes like Random-to-Top Shuffle and Random-to-Bottom Shuffle, as well as enhanced versions of Top-Tabled Sort and Fast-Tabled Sort, specifically Enhanced Top-Tabled Sort and Enhanced Fast-Tabled Sort. Our analysis centers on the coadjoint orbits within the area-preserving diffeomorphism group of ${\mathbb R}^2$ defined by these structures. We demonstrate that the corresponding polarization subgroup comprises diffeomorphisms that maintain the loop as a set; consequently, the resulting configuration space consists of loops enclosing a fixed area. Furthermore, we examine the degrees of freedom associated with the movement and deformation of such vortex loops and argue that their dynamics may be governed by an effective dynamics principle. To support this, we calculate the corresponding symplectic structure and integrate this framework with existing theories concerning point vortices and vortex sheets. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance where a point-like topology generates a finite-dimensional coadjoint orbit. This research is primarily motivated by and applicable to point-vortex-like configurations, including applied mathematical models of quantum mechanics and field theory. Extending our methodology to point vortices with a fixed number $S$ of zero-isolines—representing a finite system of particles with fixed momentum—yields results of significant theoretical interest. In this context, the resulting configuration space corresponds to a symmetric space, specifically a generalized flag manifold, which may hold potential relevance for mathematical physics. Furthermore, our findings directly inform an ongoing effort to build a coherent theory for point vortices exhibiting self-organization and symmetry breaking. This body of relevant research, which often relies on simplified models, is briefly contextualized at the conclusion of this work. Additionally, to ensure self-containment, we provide an overview of fundamental concepts and definitions regarding coadjoint orbits, polarization subgroups, and configuration spaces. Finally, to our knowledge, this paper also constitutes the inaugural attempt to numerically simulate the dynamics of vorticity configurations featuring both cusps and corners. This is achieved by deriving specific extensions of standard methods utilized in point-vortex theory and large-eddy simulations. These numerical techniques are directly applicable to various other problems involving point vortices, vortex sheets, and free boundaries. The direct implications of our research are detailed in a companion paper (M. L\'{e}onoreau and S. Brunazo, ArXiv:1808.00823).

a causal parameter typically necessitates assumptions beyond the standard confounding requirements. ATE estimation typically relies on two policy-relevant concepts: Positivity and Continuity. While Positivity addresses practical data collection, Continability manages the influence of extreme covariate values (e.g., high income) that are crucial for ATE estimation but uncommon for decision-making. Violations of the Positivity assumption are typically addressed by restricting the ATE estimation to the region where data exists (the Continuity region), resulting in the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE). Consequently, the problem of ATE estimation is reduced to two tasks: (A) determining the boundary of the Continuity region, and (B) estimating the CATE within that region. Problem (A) can be formulated as accessing an oracle through sequential policy-making. We propose two approaches to tackle this: the first involves making contextual decisions to estimate the boundary of the Continuity region, and the second estimates the boundary of this region within a bandit framework. For both methods, we provide theoretical analysis of the expected number of treatments missed (below the boundary) and the expected CATE estimation error within the Continuity region. We validate these proposals with numerical experiments that confirm our theoretical assertions. Additionally, we extend the first approach to handle scenarios where responses may be censored. Experiments extending to tens of thousands of agents demonstrate that our methods effectively estimate the ATE even when response responses are subject to censoring. Finally, we discuss how these techniques can be integrated with Transfer Learning to leverage historical data. Overall, we believe this work offers a novel perspective on ATE estimation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/iamdanieloc/Daniel-oc.git. Our approach is referred to as \textbf{D}etecting the \textbf{C}ontinuity region (\textbf{DeCo}).

Our findings indicate that the theoretical long-time average mean flow, when corrected for wavy beam thickness, aligns remarkably well with the LDV-measured wavy mean flow. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transverse (radial) wavenumber of the wavy beam increases with the rotation rate of the apparatus, consistent with prior experimental reports. By extending the theoretical mean flow to include time-dependent perturbations, we provide a framework to decompose the system's total flow into its constituent parts: the mean flow, temporal fluctuations, and spatial fluctuations. This comprehensive analysis allows for a distinction between wavy beams and true mean flow features based on their time and space dependencies. Ultimately, our study resolves the long-standing debate regarding mean flow morphology in this system, confirming that the wavy structure detected directly by LDV represents the actual mean flow, thereby validating nearly three decades of theoretical predictions. The accurate agreement between LDV and theory also substantiates the wavy beam theory's effectiveness in modeling mean flow formation. Building on this, we outline the methodology for deriving exact analytical expressions for mean flow bifurcations and their connection to baroclinic instability, offering a theoretical approach to predict the boundary between laminar and turbulent regimes in this model system. We demonstrate how barrier heights calculated via perturbation theory or optimal perturbation theory can account for the experimentally observed total transition threshold. Additionally, we extend the bifurcation analysis to include spatial fluctuations, enabling predictions of total transition thresholds based on total wavenumbers and offering an explanation for the empirically derived "butterfly diagram." These extensions may aid in the theoretical interpretation of future experimental data regarding turbulent flow transitions. Building on this research, a companion paper will provide a broader overview of the wavy beam theory's primary achievements and outline its foundational assumptions. Determining the equation of state (EOS) for dense nuclear matter is a central challenge in nuclear astrophysics. Recent theoretical investigations have focused on the impact of short-range correlations (SRC) on the EOS. However, a definitive verification of these SRC effects remains difficult, as it would require direct measurement of nuclear reaction cross sections sensitive to such correlations. This work examines the effect of SRC on neutron star matter EOS utilizing world SRC data. We find that a power-law EOS remains robust when constrained by SRC data. Although the exact functional form is not uniquely determined, we demonstrate that any parametric power-law EOS consistent with SRC data can be transformed into any other via suitable polytropic indices. Our analysis confirms that power-law forms accurately represent neutron star matter EOS. Moreover, we show that SRC data impose stricter constraints on theoretical EOS models than do nuclear binding energies. Any proposed EOS deviating from a power-law structure must provide explicit justification. Finally, our findings have essential implications for gravitational wave astronomy.

\section{Introduction}

The discovery of exotic hadrons—such as tetraquarks, molecular states, and glueballs—by the LHCb collaboration\cite{LCB:exotics} has spurred renewed theoretical and theoretical-data analysis efforts. A comprehensive understanding of exotic hadrons relies critically on properties like their masses and decay widths. Although extensive searches for nonet $D$ and $B$ mesons are underway, only ground-state $S$-wave and excited-state $P$-wave mesons have been firmly established, leaving the experimental status of $D$ and $B$ mesons in higher waves ($G$-wave, $F$-wave, etc.) ambiguous. Consequently, predicting the spectral properties of these mesons remains significant.

Existing predictions for $D$ and $B$ meson spectra—including $S$-, $P$-, $D$-wave, and recently $G$-wave states—are widespread. However, reliable predictions for $F$-wave bottom mesons remain scarce. This paper aims to predict the mass spectrum and decay widths of $F$-wave bottom mesons.

Alternatively, the Quark-Meson duality model \cite{QMD} utilizes a collective coordinate method to obtain Regge trajectories. The effective field theory approach, however, offers superior control over systematic uncertainties.

This paper investigates Szabados's conjecture. Initially, we demonstrate that it suffices to examine minimal periodic decompositions where each periodic configuration operates on a finite alphabet. Subsequently, we establish that the conjecture is valid for a broad class of configurations, encompassing all not fully periodic configurations with low convex pattern complexity. Additionally, we provide several constructions of periodic decompositions where certain nonexpansive lines fail to contain any period, although they do contain preimages of those periods. Finally, we present a construction of a periodic decomposition wherein the set of nonexpansive lines is strictly smaller than the set of lines that contain at least one period from a periodic decomposition. These findings rely on a novel technique involving the construction of periodic decompositions from given words, alongside some foundational observations regarding nonexpansive lines. Specifically, we demonstrate that the problem reduces to identifying suitable words for the "slots" in a framework of fixed slots. We further argue that nonexpansive lines are determined by the arrangements of these slots and that their structure can be modeled using a directed graph, where vertices represent the slots and edges indicate that one set of slots is a shift of another. Our construction involves carefully selecting words to ensure the existence or non-existence of specific edges in this graph. This methodology is broadly applicable and may prove useful in other contexts. In particular, it enables the demonstration that the collection of nonexpansive lines is generally not a convex set. These findings suggest that such Orton-time cosmological models, potentially representing our universe, may have originated from initial conditions closely matching the identified initial parameters. Consequently, the Orton time framework offers a plausible temporal dimension capable of addressing the standard cosmological singularities of $\rho$ and curvature. The extremality correction is then extracted from the $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^0)$ term in the gravitational action. A key aspect of this technique is the appropriate selection of metric perturbations, which must respect specific asymptotic boundary conditions that permit a controlled transition from black holes to extremal black holes. We review several prominent arguments found in the literature that justify the necessity of complex formalism and offer additional insights by introducing alternative perspectives. Our goal is to reinforce the challenging pedagogical task of explaining why Quantum Mechanics requires complex numbers. Specifically, we present four distinct approaches to quantum reconstruction and highlight their commonalities and differences. In Approach A, we rely on propositions and states as the formal foundation of quantum theory, applying this to qubits and spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ systems. In Approach B, we prioritize events, operators, and states, listing the axiomatic postulates of quantum mechanics and deriving the complex field as an unavoidable consequence in a unique manner. In Approach C, we construct quantum theory from probabilities associated with maximal measurements on state preparations and from state re-preparation following maximal measurements, again showing the emergence of complex numbers. Finally, Approach D examines whether probabilities arising from specific measurement-repreparation cycles in qubits can uniquely determine the quantum state; we demonstrate that they can, provided the single-qubit Bloch sphere is formed from all possible re-preparations after initial preparations, thereby establishing the complex field. By presenting these four complementary methods, we aim to clarify both the motivations and pathways for reconstructing quantum theory from its probabilistic core, revealing how the complex field naturally emerges in each framework. Together, these approaches address longstanding challenges and open new routes to derive the complex field and quantum formalism directly from probability axioms, potentially yielding novel perspectives on fundamental questions in quantum foundations. We conclude by listing other reconstruction methods that also lead to the complex field and listing references that explore alternative approaches to quantum reconstruction. This work underscores that complex numbers are an intrinsic part of quantum theory, emerging through various rigorous and conceptually clear derivations from core postulates, and should not be overlooked in quantum education. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the complex field is not required when formulating quantum theory over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q(p)$, where $p$ is a prime and $q=p^r$ for some integer $r \geq 2$, although the physical interpretation of quantum probabilities remains unclear in such cases.

{\bf Keywords:} Quantum Reconstruction, Complex Numbers, Finite Fields, Quantum Foundations, Pedagogical Aspects of Quantum Mechanics.

This equivalence implies that the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property is a topological invariant and identifies the largest class of non-Tychonoff spaces possessing this property, which includes all locally compact Hausdorff spaces. The paper also explores variations of the CSHP, including normal and compact compactly supported homeomorphism stability, and investigates related topologies on homeomorphism groups, such as the topology of compact convergence. Notably, the compacts supported homeomorphism stability of the product of the Long Line with the Integers confirms the validity of a conjecture by M. Ra\v{c}i\'c. The findings also have implications for questions originally posed by J. Isbell.

For the lightest subhalo mass, our model reprodules the JWST/NGTS observed temperature depression, moving the cooling flow onto the merger axis and reducing its intensity to match observations. Intermediate cluster halo masses result in intermediate cooling flow characteristics, but a new feature emerges: a secondary temperature dip away from the merger axis caused by gas expansion in the wake of the subhalo. Finally, ray-tracing through simulated X-ray maps allows for the reconstruction of projected temperature images that replicate the key cooling flow features seen in JWST data. In this paper, we formulate an economic model based on the ideas of both CPs and ISPs, predicting the conditions under which these protocols could be widely adopted. While the CP's incentive to invest is clear, the critical question remains: why should an ISP want to invest? Although one might expect an ISP to invest more when shouldering a smaller cost share, we rigorously demonstrate the opposite: under reasonable assumptions, an ISP's total investment increases as its cost share of the investment money rises. Furthermore, we reveal a counter-intuitive outcome: when total investment is higher, demand for the content can decrease. These findings explain the disparity between the robust theoretical argument for the protocol and its sparse practical adoption, as our results indicate that CPs may achieve greater demand and profits by forgoing investment contributions to the ISP. Finally, we extend this analysis to scenarios involving multiple ISPs, yielding analogous conclusions.

Recently, we introduced a method to reconstruct the inflationary background by training a neural network on simulation data, wherein the network input consists of the scalar power spectrum and its first two derivatives, evaluated at a specific scale $k_*$, while the output is the corresponding slow-roll parameters. In this work, we generalize that approach to include derivatives of the tensor power spectrum, demonstrating that incorporating them alongside the scalar spectrum and their shared derivative significantly enhances reconstruction accuracy without increasing model bias. Additionally, we investigate whether neural networks can be employed to directly map from the scalar spectrum to the inflationary background. We show that such learning is feasible and capable of improving upon existing analytic methods, although it still requires training data generated by analytic reconstruction techniques. Our results imply that neural networks can be utilized to reconstruct inflationary backgrounds from observed scalar and tensor perturbations, provided that sufficiently rare large-scale modes are available to reduce uncertainties in the spectrum's large-$k_*$ behavior. However, due to current limitations in numerical simulations, current implementations remain less accurate than analytic methods.

Utilizing a formal Bayesian inference approach, we developed continuous-time discrete-event stochastic processes alongside associated continuous stochastic differential equation approximations that capture the dynamics of adaptive sensory mechanisms. This processing occurs during the intervals between event pairs, with system adaptation reflected in the updated probability distributions of the event pairs themselves. We characterized a family of general adaptive sensing systems applicable to diverse fields, including sensory biology and specific microphones or sonar devices that adjust their fields of view via motion. Generally, such systems anticipate unobserved random variables and adapt their measurement strategies based on prior data to gather new, independent information. By employing a generic Shannon information gain metric, we identified two distinct mechanisms that achieve this objective: temporal and structural. Temporal sensing involves discrete measurements separated by both deterministic and random intervals; the system adapts its timing to sample when uncertainty is highest and when fluctuations are uncorrelated with previous samples. Structural sensing relies on directional or positional measurements; adaptation manifests as an ability to orient toward regions of prior uncertainty while accounting for spatial correlations between variables. The continuous stochastic differential equation formulations provide rigorous conditions under which these processes reach informational equilibrium and converge exponentially fast to their stationary distributions. Furthermore, we derived analytical expressions for key performance indicators, including the invariant uncertainty distributions and the long-term average information gain rates achieved by adaptive systems compared to their non-adaptive counterparts. Finally, although statistical properties and motion vary, biological sensory systems and controlled artificial systems appear to operate near comparable levels of average uncertainty and information gain, both executing structural active sensing with roughly constant time-averaged motion speeds. Non-adaptive sensors typically maintain significantly lower average motion speeds. These findings suggest that while motion speed alone is an unreliable indicator of adaptation, the ratio of time-averaged to invariant motion speed may serve as a more effective metric for assessing adaptation across different systems. This is particularly relevant for sensory systems exhibiting self-similar uncertainty distributions, where the motion speed ratio remains approximately constant and independent of motion characteristics or uncertainty levels. Although extensive mathematical analysis is complete, determining exact performance metrics numerically remains challenging due to difficulties in analytically evaluating high-order non-central moments of invariant variable distributions and integrals over exponential transition density functions. To address this, we introduced a new dimensionless parameter, the "sloppiness" of the stochastic system, alongside computational and approximation methods to derive performance metrics with high precision. This study focuses on stochastic processes characterized by high entropy production, specifically examining the sign of this production within a defined timeframe $t$. We demonstrate that the stochastic process resulting from this binary observation behaves asymptotically as a strong mixing process. We further establish practical formulas for key observables of such strong mixing processes and utilize these to derive estimates for the rate of decay of correlations, as well as bounds for the spectral gap and the decay of the fundamental coefficient in the Feynman-Hellmann formula, all expressed in terms of $t$ and the system's entropy production. Additionally, we prove that the fundamental coefficient remains positive and establish inequalities involving it. These findings enable the analysis of fundamental properties for thermodynamic processes with large entropy production. Furthermore, we apply these results to derive a novel lower bound for the Prandtl number and to elucidate the behavior of fundamental operators within the framework of non-equilibrium thermodynamics. Finally, we demonstrate that the time-dependent effective Hamiltonian, which incorporates three control fields and exhibits anti-symmetric time dependence, is Hermitian. The results regarding strong mixing processes facilitate the estimation of norms and inequalities associated with this Hamiltonian, thereby providing estimates for thermodynamic quantities such as the coefficient of thermal conductivity, the Prandtl number, and the transport coefficient. This work establishes a new framework for investigating thermodynamic properties and fundamental operators within the theory of nonequilibrium processes. Building on recent successes with DCNNs in medical image analysis, we investigate their application to segmenting retinal layers in OCT images—a complex yet critical task for early disease detection. Our study compares DCNNs trained from scratch with those employing transfer learning, revealing that transfer learning yields substantial improvements. We further examine the impact of using unlabeled data to pretrain models via semi-supervised techniques, though this approach did not provide significant advantages over transfer learning. We demonstrate that high-quality retinal layer segmentation is achievable with DCNNs through the integration of transfer learning and ensembling, thereby enabling more precise analysis of retinal structures.

However, we demonstrate that intensity-dependent dispersion yields novel features in the stability analysis of black solitons. Specifically, the spectral stability problem admits only isolated eigenvalues along the imaginary axis. Furthermore, energy variational methods confirm the spectral stability of these black solitons. We propose employing variational autoencoders (VAEs) to learn a continuous latent representation of discrete switch configurations. This enables optimization over a smooth intermediate space, facilitating hybrid optimization that simultaneously tunes continuous control variables and discrete switch settings. **I. INTRODUCTION**

The formation of exciton-polariton condensates within microcavities presents a unique platform at the intersection of superfluidity, non-equilibrium, and spin-orbital coupling. These properties stem from weak light-matter coupling, leakage losses, and pump-driven non-equilibrium conditions. Consequently, exciton-polariton condensates are valuable for investigating fundamental questions regarding spin-orbital quantum simulation and many-body physics. Furthermore, their rapid recombination enables efficient, low-threshold sources of integrated nonlinear and single photons, which are essential components for quantum information processing. This work examines how anisotropic optical trapping facilitates control over polariton pair spin and linear polarization propagation. Specifically, we show that engineering the in-plane anisotropy of the trap allows for the creation of a ground state featuring spin-orbital coupling, the generation of linearly polarized polariton pairs, and an increase in the compressibility of the condensate anisotropy. This setup is particularly promising for researching fundamental properties of polariton condensation and quantum information applications utilizing polariton-based qubits.

It can be efficiently implemented by substitlying integers with powers of two and summing the results, where the exponents correspond to a sparse binary representation of the multiplication constants. Since this exponent sequence must be optimized for every MCM instance, numerous algorithms have been developed to address this challenge. VSP integrates an MPC engine built on any-partitioned secret sharing (APSS) with a Security Layer that shields both participants and underlying resources from physical attacks. This Security Layer employs a nested redundancy framework across multiple levels, utilizing error detection and correction across two functional layers: the Infrastructure Security Layer (ISL) and the Execution Security Layer (ISXL). The ISL manages error control among more than three execution levels: Encryption Redundancy (ER), Functional Redundancy (FR), and Mission Redundancy (MR). To ensure robustness against physical attacks, the ISL validates each layer through three independent methods: Embedded Memory Ring Oscillator (eMRO) frequency monitoring, Data Injection Verification (DIV), and Random Injection (RI). Every level operates within an isolated hardware region defined by fence circuits and secured via Lock Step FR and Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR). Furthermore, the APSS layer leverages any-partitioned secret sharing to protect secrets residing in Flash Memory Secure Elements (MSECs) or RAM Secure Elements (RMSECs) from physical extraction. We present a secure storage architecture based on Share on Read (SOR) enabled MSECs and outline two protocols: the Secure Storage (SS) protocol for protected RAM access and the Flash Secure Storage (FSS) protocol for persistent data management. These schemes guarantee that even if an adversary extracts all persistent secrets from RMSECs and MSECs, the security protocol remains unbreached. To enhance VSP's practicality, we developed a multi-party compilation framework based on any-partitioned secret sharing, which automatically generates a multi-party comparison (MPC) protocol from annotated C source code. This framework supports any partitioning strategy, including threshold any-partitioned secret sharing (APSS), and produces an executable MPC binary that directly runs on the MPC engine. Execution performance was evaluated using three benchmark applications: a multi-party comparison function, a cryptographic hash function, and RSA encryption. Results demonstrate that, assuming no physical attack occurs, the secured applications achieve speedups of 1.8x to 6.7x compared to non-secured counterparts. Testing with programmable Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) revealed that the security layers introduce less than 3% overhead to the SEC level and approximately 10% to the MPC level. The objective is to determine whether a random feasible solution serves as an $\epsilon$-approximation to the optimal solution with high probability when the number of constraints per item is sufficiently small. Although random algorithms have historically been effective for specific CSPs, they have failed in general optimization settings, notably failing for integer programming. However, for PTASes utilizing linear programming relaxations, random algorithmic approaches have consistently succeeded.

For general optimization problems, this paper establishes conditions under which a random algorithm achieves a PTAS. It demonstrates that if a feasible solution randomization vector exists such that the associated random integer program remains feasible while introducing minimal additional constraints, then a PTAS can be formulated. Conversely, it is shown that if a feasible solution randomization matrix exists where the expected number of fractional integers in the resulting random integer program is sublinear, then an PTAS is achievable.

Each item in a general optimization problem can be modeled as a vector of nonnegative integers, potentially unbounded, assigned random values with specified distributions. The initial section focuses on problems with a single constraint per item, demonstrating how to construct a feasible solution randomization vector that ensures expected objective function linearity. The second section examines general optimization problems, illustrating methods to design a randomization matrix that minimizes the count of fractional integers. It proves that for many distribution types, this approach yields an PTAS, including cases with a constant number of constraints per item.

Generally, randomizing item selections increases the number of constraints, as varying selections may lead to different outcomes. Consequently, additional constraints are necessary to ensure all selected items produce identical results. The study begins by analyzing general optimization problems with a fixed number of outcomes, indicating how to create a randomization matrix that minimizes fractional integers. This methodology has already succeeded for generalized assignment problems, clustering, multi-commodity integer flows, minimum latency problem, maximum coverage problem, generalized Steiner tree problem, set partitioning problem, and generalized minimum cost multicut problem.

The analysis of problems with a limited number of states per item reveals that randomization matrices can be constructed with a sublinear count of fractional integers, even when some entries remain strictly fractional. This approach employs an approach similar to the first method, utilizing a randomization matrix with only a limited number of fractional integers. We address this by employing the abstract machine principle, which emphasizes simplicity, plausibility, and explicitness, and requires adjustments only when confronted with conflicting complexity outcomes. This paper introduces ConContextNet, a flexible pipeline designed to integrate context-aware models into problem-specific scenarios. The system begins with a feedforward network optimized for the primary task; if analysis of training data or prior work indicates that additional context would benefit the specific problem, the network is augmented with recurrent connections tailored to maximize performance by exploiting that context. Conversely, if the task does not benefit from context, the system remains strictly feedforward. By selectively applying recurrent enhancements only when advantageous, ConContextNet delivers superior performance across diverse tasks compared to purely feedforward architectures and matches the accuracy of fully recurrent systems that are less adaptable. Consequently, ConContextNet achieves state-of-the-art results in object recognition, scene flow estimation, and visual question answering.

We define the transitivity degree of $X$ as the maximal integer $m$ for which the $\text{Aut}(X)$-action on $X$ is $m$-transitive; if the action is $m$-transitive for every $m$, the degree is infinite. In this work, we calculate the transitivity degree for all quasi-affine toric varieties and numerous homogeneous spaces of algebraic groups, while also examining a conjecture and several open questions concerning transitivity degrees.

We introduce the concept of the flag variety associated with a homogeneous space $G/H$, denoted $\text{Flag}(G/H)$. For any homogeneous space $X$ of a reductive group $G$, we establish that $\text{Flag}(G/H)$ is non-empty if and only if $X$ achieves infinite transitivity degree. Furthermore, we derive necessary conditions for a variety to possess maximal transitivity degree. Specifically, we prove that if $X$ attains maximal transitivity degree, then $\text{Flag}(X)$ must be non-empty and $\text{Aut}(X)$-homogeneous. As an application, we demonstrate that the transitivity degree of $X$ cannot exceed the rank加一 of $G$ when $X$ has maximal degree, and that the transitivity degree of a homogeneous affine cone over $X$ equals the degree of $X$ plus one.

We also determine the transitivity degrees for all homogeneous cone curves and homogeneous surfaces of minimal non-negative logarithmic Minaka-Mori degree. Additionally, we prove that the affine cone over the Segre embedding of $\mathbb{P}^2\times \mathbb{P}^2$ possesses transitivity degree three, thereby providing the first known example of a $\text{Aut}(X)$-homogeneous variety that does not have maximal transitivity degree. Finally, as an appendix, we present an algorithm to construct irreducible representations with highest weight $\lambda$ of the algebraic group $\text{SL}_{n+1}$ that yield non-empty flag varieties, along with necessary conditions for the flag variety $\text{Flag} (G/H)$ to be non-empty. This construction relies on descent theory applied to principal bundles.

P.\ Malliavin \cite{P.Malliavin} introduced a powerful framework for deriving Lévy-Khintchine formulas for functionals of Markov processes, which has since become an essential instrument in probability theory. Concurrently, P.\ Malliavin and M.\ Yor \cite{Malliavin} developed stochastic calculus for multiple Wiener spaces, defining operators that measure the sensitivity of random variables relative to past trajectories of Brownian motion. Building on this, J.\ Zhang \cite{zhang2010double} defined $p$-measure change and generated measures to characterize the $p$-exponential change of measures for real-valued Brownian motion. These concepts have since been generalized to various stochastic processes and diverse closed subspaces of multiple Wiener spaces.

While centralized coded caching aims to minimize transmission duration in delay-sensitive networks, distributed gradient descent (CGD) seeks to reduce latency in time-sensitive environments. This paper demonstrates that these two distinct areas are deeply connected. Specifically, we show that for any CGC scheme achieving a given rate at a certain cache size, a corresponding CGD method exists that matches this scheme's number of iterations and periteration complexity. More broadly, any improvement in CGD performance can be leveraged to enhance coded caching schemes. We begin by outlining the relationship between CGC and CGD and substantiating this link through a review of existing literature on coded caching. Subsequently, we propose a novel progressive coded caching scheme that achieves both lower rates and reduced transcoder complexity compared to the Separate File Caching (SFC) baseline. Finally, we suggest an application of the proposed progressive scheme to derive a new CGD approach. Our findings indicate that the new method yields significant gains over SFC-based CGD, confirming that innovative coded caching designs can indeed drive substantial enhancements in CGD efficiency. Throughout this work, we emphasize that coded caching serves not only as a mechanism to decrease transmission loads in communication systems but also as a computational framework for addressing latency-critical tasks in large-scale distributed environments. We argue that recognizing this dual role will inspire further innovations in coded caching and enable the adaptation of diverse distributed computing challenges to well-established coded caching frameworks. Furthermore, we contend that a more profound understanding of the relationship between CGC and CGD will facilitate the rapid development of novel, intelligent, and proactive distributed latency-sensitive computing schemes capable of adapting to fluctuating network conditions. In conclusion, we believe that both theoretical and practical research in coded caching should explicitly address their broad applicability to distributed computing and elaborates on this connection. Additionally, we encourage coded caching scholars to maintain a clear vision of how their work advances practical distributed computing and how it establishes performance benchmarks. We also suggest that future investigations into novel coded caching schemes prioritize achieving a superior trade-off between caching complexity and reduced rates, rather than focusing solely on minimizing rates. Most importantly, we advocate for the development of rigorous evaluated benchmarks within practical distributed latency-sensitive computing environments. These benchmarks should compare various CGD approaches—ranging from pure gradient descent and proximal gradient descent to those utilizing coded caching and other distributed latency-sensitive techniques—against realistic metrics including iteration count, periteration complexity, communication complexity, and convergence rates. We also plan to extend our analysis to other latency-sensitive distributed computing scenarios to establish coded caching as a fundamental

Numerical experiments confirm the method's effectiveness and derive an explicit formula for the operator in vectorized notation for practical implementation. Finally, the paper presents a systematic approach for constructing quasi-interpolation schemes using hyperbolic or other quasi-linear functions derived from linear interpolation. The pulsar CTTE J1721-3001, located at a distance of approximately 2.5 kpc, is the second pulsar identified as hosting such a gamma-ray halo, distinguished by an unusually large emission region. This study investigates the characteristics of J1721-3001 by examining its high-energy spectrum, spatial distribution, and morphology. We demonstrate that fitting the high-energy (GeV) portion of the spectrum requires either a cutoff energy ($E_{cut}$) of roughly 10 TeV or a break energy ($E_{br}$) at approximately 1 TeV. The findings indicate that this source exhibits long-term variability, with the total gamma-ray flux varying by a factor of more than 3 across observations separated by at least one year. Furthermore, we present evidence suggesting variability in the source's spatial distribution on timescales of several months to a year, a phenomenon potentially attributable to scattering effects. Additionally, J1721-3001 displays extended tails reaching beyond 10 pc, a trait shared by only about 10% of pulsar halos. Collectively, these results highlight significant high-energy emission components in J1721-3001 on both sub- and super-parsec scales. The source's high energy content and extended morphology offer valuable insights into gamma-ray production and diffusion mechanisms occurring on scales exceeding 1 pc. Furthermore, J1721-3001 may serve as an ideal candidate for testing various models of pulsar halos, as well as for exploring connections between neutron stars and large-scale gamma-ray structures. Finally, this source provides critical data points for constraining parameters in diffusion models, particularly given its significant distance from the pulsar's position.

Current approaches typically rely on extensive historical data to build predictive models. In contrast, this study addresses scenarios where transportation data is scarce, offering an alternative solution without requiring large datasets. We propose a novel called-based semantic network-based (SNN)-based prediction model capable of estimating headway distributions for signal timing optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and maintains robustness even with limited data. Furthermore, the SNN-based approach facilitates an explicit representation of called-based headways, thereby providing a clearer understanding of their operational characteristics and system dynamics. This explicit nature enables the automatic design of control strategies, which will be explored in future research. Ultimately, this work advances the sustainability of transportation operations and contributes to intelligent and adaptive transportation systems suitable for Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) environments. The source code and data used in this research are accessible at https://github.com/MohammadFatehi1999/Call-Based-Headway-Prediction-Model.

We examine the direct generation of this memory at second order during and immediately after the merger, bypassing the traditional "preliminary memory" phase. Our findings suggest that second-order preliminary gravitational wave memory largely cancels out for standard binary black hole systems, meaning the majority of observers will perceive only the true gravitational wave memory. However, most existing sessions originate from laboratory settings, resulting in limited information entropy. This paper introduces the concept of Cross-Session Information (CSI), defined as information gained when merging two sessions. We aim to maximize the average CSI gained when merging any two sessions within a recommendation system. To achieve this, we propose InfoCross, a novel cross-session recommendation framework that selects a new session candidate for each existing one to maximize their CSI. InfoCross achieves this by training a CSI estimator using attention mechanisms on session pairs within a training dataset. Extensive experiments across multiple public datasets demonstrate that InfoCross significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art session-based recommenders in multi-session scenarios by more than 10%. To enhance computational efficiency, we propose constraint-reduced decentralized model predictive control (DMPC) frameworks. Addressing the high computational cost typically associated with DMPC, we introduce a time-varying parameterization strategy that enables the solution of each agent's local optimization problem in closed form, thereby ensuring real-time applicability. We evaluate two distinct DMPC formulations: one utilizing a parameterized approximate cost function and another employing a reparameterized cost function. Classical methods fail for stochastic control problems driven by fractional Brownian motion because the process lacks both Markov properties and the semi-martingale structure. Nevertheless, by employing fractional White noise calculus alongside specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures, we derive a comprehensive theory of backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) involving delays and fractional Brownian motion. This paper applies that theory to resolve the mentioned optimal control problem, deriving necessary conditions for optimality in terms of a coupled system of coupled stochastic-delay differential equations involving advanced variables. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for BSDEs containing delayed terms by utilizing novel estimation techniques for these equations. Finally, our approach extends directly to stochastic delay partial differential equations (PDEs) as demonstrated in a companion paper (arXiv:2008.00883v1). This represents the first time BSDEs involving stochastic delay terms and fractional Brownian motion have been utilized to obtain necessary conditions for optimality in an optimal control problem featuring distributed delays within both state and control variables. Moreover, the derived necessary conditions constitute a generalized Pontryagin maximum principle applicable to BSDEs with fractional Brownian motion containing delays, thereby extending the classical result from \cite{B1}. This represents the most significant advancement achieved to date in the field of fractional stochastic control problems distributed delays.

By applying an in-plane magnetic field, the in-plane critical stiffness in this square-lattice system approaches zero. This behavior mirrors the temperature-dependent vanishing of critical stiffness observed in isotropic He-3 ferromagnets near the BKT transition, marking the first time such physics has been captured in an antiferromagnetic exchange-coupled, spin-1 insulator. Utilizing magnetic torque data, we extract field-dependent critical stiffness and field-ordering temperatures. Furthermore, fitting the critical stiffness as a function of temperature yields an exponent $\nu\theta$ that aligns well with theoretical predictions for the 2D BKT transition. These measurements provide novel constraints on the theoretical understanding of strongly anisotropic, low-dimensional magnetic systems undergoing quantum-to-classical insulator-to-ferromagnetic long-range order crossover. The findings also have potential relevance to ultrathin B$_2$-structured FeGe films, which exhibit comparable magnetic phase diagrams. This categorization of critical behavior in strongly anisotropic ferromagnets is also expected to apply to other spin-1 ferromagnetic insulators, offering a basis for future experimental investigations. This phenomenon arises when the interference between the standard charged current (CC) and a neutral current (NC) is negative, causing a particular contribution to the CP asymmetry to reverse sign depending on the mass hierarchy. We analyze the constraints imposed by CP-CSE in both normal and inverted hierarchies. In the normal hierarchy, the lightest neutrino is nearly massless, rendering the heaviest state heavily influenced by the heavyest charged current (CCO) parameter, which in turn restricts the NC parameter due to the unitarity of the extended PMNS matrix; consequently, CP-CSE is suppressed in this scenario. Conversely, in the inverted hierarchy, the heaviest neutrino is predominantly driven by the NC parameter, allowing the model to naturally accommodate a sign-enhancement effect, thereby boosting the lepton asymmetry. As a byproduct, we derive new relationships between NC and CCO parameters in both hierarchies, demonstrating that the NC region is broadly constrained regardless of the specific choice of other parameters, with particularly strong restrictions observed in the inverted hierarchy. Finally, we calculate the lepton asymmetry for the inverted hierarchy, showing that the NC parameter can be relatively large to produce a positive lepton asymmetry, and we illustrate this capability through several numerical examples. Furthermore, we provide new lower and upper bounds for both NC and CCO parameters, proving that the NC region is heavily constrained across various mass hierarchies. In conclusion, the lepton asymmetry is significantly amplified in the inverted hierarchy due to CP-CSE, and new lower and upper bounds are established for both NC and CCO parameters, independent of the specific choice of other parameters. By solving the Tsallis equation of state alongside the Einstein field equations, we derive an analytical expression for BBH parameters. Our results indicate that beyond parameters already constrained by LIGO-Virgo observations, the coupling constant $q$ is the primary factor influencing energy loss due to gravitational radiation. This research represents the initial attempt to constrain dark energy models using GW data from BBH mergers. SRAM-based True Random Number Generators (TRNGs) leverage the inherent randomness arising from read fluctuations in SRAM arrays. While recent research has enhanced these designs to ensure security and reliability, reliability remains a critical challenge. A primary cause of reliability failure is environmental noise, which can bias the traditional SRAM Read Array TRNG and lead to failures in NIST randomness tests. Standard Read Array TRNGs rely on uncontrolled internal SRAM read fluctuations and access line noise to generate random numbers; however, scaling modern processors to lower voltages and frequencies restricts supply noise fluctuations, thereby degrading performance and increasing the likelihood of NIST test failures. Although recent studies address this, they depend on specific processor implementations, limiting general applicability. Additionally, post-implementation improvements to existing TRNG designs are difficult due to access complexity. To overcome these limitations, this work integrates an RO-based enhancement into a TRNG architecture, requiring only a 2% layout modification in modern standard cell flows. The design significantly improves reliability by increasing the probability of Branch Point Fluctuation (BPF) events and is generalizable across all modern processor implementations. Furthermore, the design is scalable, allowing for a 100x increase in throughput, and results in less than a 3% area overhead, outperforming most recent TRNG solutions.

It has been observed that applying LTD to Feynman integrands yields a representation comprising solely multi-loop integrands, which can be recursively defined using features inherent to single-loop factors. This paper introduces forward-forward forward-forward forward loops by iterating the LTD relation four times on a one-loop integral featuring eight propagators. Although such highly "forward" integrals possess singular integrands that preclude direct numerical evaluation, they serve as intermediate stages in the LTD recursion and are crucial components of actual multi-loop integrands. We confirm that these forward integrals are well-defined through regularization analysis and demonstrate that their finite parts contain no singularities. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to similar "forward" integrals with fewer propagators and investigate the symmetry properties of these newly identified integrals. Finally, we examine the influence of newly discovered constants, termed forward constants, which emerge naturally from this LTD framework. Unlike $\pi$ or other mathematical constants, these forward constants appear to be process-dependent; for instance, $F_6^{(6)}$ arises specifically from six-forward integrals. Unlike Euler or generalized zeta constants, these forward constants do not seem reducible via integration by parts to standard mathematical constants. Furthermore, unlike transcendentals found in multi-loop integrands through conventional methods, many of these forward constants transcend existing theoretical bounds on transcendentality within that framework. Consequently, these forward constants constitute a new class of constants distinct from classical constants like $\zeta_n$. Finally, we explore the potential application of LTD to compute multi-loop integrands involving fewer than all external legs and its relevance to future amplitude calculations. Additionally, we propose an alternative interpretation of LTD that avoids the complications associated with "forward" integrals. This alternative formulation relies on decomposing multi-loop integrands into contributions from loops active at specific kinematic scales, referred to as loop windows. Each loop window corresponds to a Feynman integral with fewer than $L+1$ loops (where $L$ is the loop order of the amplitude), characterized by different virtualities and numerator polynomials than those in full loop factors. Unlike the conventional formulation, this approach does not require "forward" integrals as intermediate steps and can directly generate integrands with arbitrary loop orders and topology. This method enables the direct evaluation of multi-loop integrands, including those previously inaccessible through LTD, and establishes a new framework for constructing multi-loop integrands. **1. Abstract**

This article offers a direct proof of an eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional two-state quantum walks, functioning as an equivalent to the time-reversal method used in [Kim]. This direct approach enables the formulation of the eigenfunction expansion via the discrete Stokes theorem, thereby establishing the eigenfunction expansions of birth-death processes and their time reverses through the Gauss theorem instead of relying on killing rates, as seen in [Kim]. Employing this direct proof, we provide a straightforward demonstration of the hypercontractivity inequality for birth-death processes, avoiding the complications inherent in the weighted logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

This evolution is rooted in quantum field theory principles and is driven fundamentally by quantum finite-size effects. These effects arise naturally from two distinct sources: first, from boundary conditions imposed on coherent states, which generate finite-size Fock states; and second, from boundary conditions applied to thermal states, yielding quasi-thermal states. Both states are inherently thermal due to their finite sizes. This paper examines two scenarios: one where light is generated via boundary conditions on vacuum noise, resulting in quasi-thermal light, and another involving boundary conditions on a thermal bath. This deformation not only advances squeezed optomechanics but also facilitates the creation of finite-size Fock states and thermal states. We conclude by illustrating two instances where coherent states are $q$-deformed and providing illustrative examples where thermal states approach the Fock state regime. This comprehensive analysis of finite-size effects and $q$-deformation expands the theoretical foundations of squeezed and $q$-deformed optomechanics, offering novel methods to manipulate vacuum, quasi-thermal, thermal, and coherent states. These developments pave the way for novel approaches to quantum state engineering and enhance quantum information processing within optomechanical systems. Additionally, these theories support the formulation of novel approaches for quantum thermodynamics. Specifically, they enable the generation of heat, work, and energy at the nanoscale through two distinct mechanisms: boundary conditions and $q$-deformation. This capability opens pathways to investigate energy phenomena at the smallest scales. Moreover, these methods advance quantum heat engines and provide precise tools for measuring quantum heat and energy. This quantum finite-size effect underpins the concept of quantum criticality and provides a new perspective on the quantum nature of heat and light. These insights drive the search for new sources of thermal-like, thermal, coherent, and squeezed light, as well as novel approaches to quantum measurement theory. They also facilitate the study of coherent matter waves and provide precise quantization of quantum noise. This work supports quantum noise engineering and offers new techniques for detecting and measuring quantum finite-size effects. We propose that these phenomena are intrinsically linked and can be understood through the lens of information theory. Specifically, we define the negentropy of a state as a metric for its stability against mixing with other states of identical composition. We demonstrate that material phases exhibiting strong correlations, magnetism, or unusual transport properties are inherently negentropic in nature. Consequently, emerging insulating phases—often termed Mott, orbital, or hidden orders—represent instances where negentropy emerges from the self-interaction of mobile electrons within a metallic background. This framework offers a novel perspective on materials like La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_4$ and Ca$_2$IrO$_4$, which remain in debate regarding their true ground states. Furthermore, it underscores a fundamental connection between negentropy, correlation strength, and the emergence of Mott insulation: any system where electron self-interaction governs energy balance, whether attractive or repulsive, will exhibit negentropy-driven insulating behavior characteristic of Mott physics. Ultimately, we contend that negentropy may serve as a universal principle driving not only Mott physics but also various ordering transitions in diverse many-body systems. Therefore, the quest for negative free energy may be viewed as comprising two components: the removal of entropy (manifesting here as negentropy) and the release of negative energy (i.e., energy). We propose a classification of insulating transitions based on this decomposition and establish a criterion to differentiate between Mott insulators and their alternatives. Finally, we explore various testable predictions and concepts for future research.

Many transition-metal oxides, which should theoretically conduct electricity, instead behave as insulators. This drive, which we term "negentropy," was vital during the universe's early expansion and may now be essential in certain condensed-matter systems. We illustrate this using transition-metal oxides, showing that their insulating nature, magnetic ordering, and other properties—such as heavy quasiparticle formation or correlated insulating states—can be viewed as specific methods by which negentropy reduces free energy. . In recent years, investigation into stochastic processes driven by self-organization has gained significant traction. This paper examines a stochastic process occurring within a bounded domain, specifically addressing questions regarding first exit times and paths relative to that domain. We utilize a model applicable across various physical contexts, featuring two key characteristics: (i) the process remains confined within the domain, and (ii) it exhibits preferential diffusion, where the probability of leaving the domain increases as the process approaches the boundary. This preferential diffusion is commonly observed near boundaries in systems such as fluids, gases, and liquids. Although this model has been previously studied, our analysis addresses novel mathematical challenges. We derive analytical expressions for the probability density of first exit times, expected values of these times, and the probability of exiting through specific segments. For systems with stationary distributions, we further provide expressions for the fractional moment of the residence time, alongside formulas for mean square displacement and autocorrelation. We demonstrate the applicability of these results through a specific boundary layer stochastic process. Finally, our findings are validated numerically using Monte Carlo simulations.

We begin by constructing a cryptocurrency trading network, where nodes represent individual cryptocurrencies and links denote Granger causality derived from their log returns across multiple time scales. By systematically selecting market caps to identify a representative subset, we demonstrate that this network is surprisingly sparse, exhibiting distinct core-periphery structure with negatively correlated log returns in core nodes. Next, we analyze short-term dynamics using transfer entropy, revealing that while peripheral peripherals act as net receivers, core core nodes function as net exporters of information. Finally, we explore dynamics across different time scales via mutual information, showing that the network's structural characteristics become more pronounced as the observation window expands. Overall, our findings indicate that cryptocurrency trading networks are more interconnected than previously thought, with significant connections emerging under certain conditions. These links facilitate the propagation of information, suggesting that certain cryptocurrencies monitor and learn from others to optimize trading decisions. This core-periphery architecture implies that fluctuations propagate sequentially from the periphery to the core, a mechanism likely driven by speculative behavior. These results hold robustness across various methodologies and provide crucial insights for understanding similar markets. Crucially, this reveals that certain cryptocurrencies possess monitoring capacities, acting as information hubs.

Recent research has revealed log-normal heavy tails and increased volatility as cryptocurrency adoption grows. This paper presents empirical evidence of increased complexity using the network formed by pairwise mutual information of optimal forecasting models across various time scales. Employing multiple evaluation metrics, including Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) and Shannon entropy, we demonstrate a robust linear correlation between the Kolmogorov-Smirnov metric and the ratio ($\sigma/\mu$) of return volatility to the mean of the log-Signal, confirming log-normal tails grow stronger with adoption. Furthermore, we show that the proportion of the variance unexplained by linear regression between two models' forecast errors rises significantly with adoption, serving as a metric for pairwise mutual information. We explore the resulting network structure, proving its self-similarity and characterizing it via a time-varying degree distribution. Additionally, we examine temporal dynamics using multiple metrics, proving that intra-day networks are sparser than weekly ones, noting that day-level sparsity increases substantially with adoption. Finally, we identify periods of market stress marked by higher volatility and greater complexity.

We introduce a deep learning framework that learns the mapping from tomographic data to the quantum state through training on data generated from known states. This approach eliminates the need for manual feature engineering, as the algorithm autonomously acquires the necessary information during the training phase. Additionally, our method determines the quantum state directly from measurement outcomes, streamlining the quantum inverse problem. We evaluate the accuracy of this deep learning-based QST on both simulated and experimental tomographic data obtained from photonic qubits, comparing these experimental findings against earlier reported results. Overall, our findings demonstrate that deep learning offers a potent and promising strategy for QST, applicable to both photonic and photonic-assisted qubit systems. Our results indicate that the proposed approach is well-suited for practical, real-world applications, especially given its efficiency in reducing computational time and complexity. Our studies suggest that this machine learning-driven QST can be extended to higher-dimensional quantum systems, making it an attractive option for numerous quantum information processing tasks. By demonstrating the viability of DNNs for QST, our research paves the way for future exploration of advanced learning and neural network techniques in quantum state reconstruction. Furthermore, our research emphasizes the utility of deep learning in addressing inverse problems, making it relevant to diverse fields in science and engineering. We believe this research will assist scientists in both academia and industry as they develop their own quantum machine learning projects. Our ultimate goal is to enable quantum machines to infer patterns and solve tomographic data analysis tasks. By leveraging our quantum-state recovery algorithms, we aim to facilitate the swift learning and implementation of QST. We anticipate that our research will enable scientists to establish their own quantum machine learning initiatives and assist them in navigating the complexities associated with this field. This paper introduces a novel, efficient synthesis algorithm for such filters in these environments. Specifically, we address high-level safety in partially observable settings where motion planning is constrained by low-level requirements like smoothness during intermediate stages. Our approach models this problem as a synthesis task on a hybrid automaton, wherein modes represent belief states of the partially observable system and transitions encompass both discrete and continuous inputs. We define two distinct safety objectives: (1) high-level safety defined by distinguishing between unsafe and safe belief states, and (2) high-level safety defined by distinguishing between unsafe and safe trajectories. By formally encoding this problem as a reach-avoid synthesis task on the hybrid automaton, we demonstrate that high-level safety can be guaranteed while minimizing control effort during transient phases. Our solution is derived through a sequence of transformations yielding either a finite-state automaton or a parameterized control law. We validate the applicability of this synthesis method across various challenging scenarios, including new examples involving distinction between potentially unsafe trajectories and the separation of potentially unsafe vehicles. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/danielkrahulc/ctrl_safe_filters.

Problem Statement

Formal Methods offer reliable techniques for designing control systems that safely navigate uncertain, dynamic environments. Their value becomes particularly evident when integrating potentially unsafe learning-based controllers into critical systems where failure is unacceptable. In such contexts, the primary goal is to ensure that the final trajectory remains safe, even if the interim trajectory is not. Furthermore, because the environment is often only partially observable, the controller must maintain and synthesize a belief state that accurately reflects its knowledge of the current situation.

To address these needs, we developed and refined two variants of safety filters over time. The earlier version, Control Barrier Function-based Trajectory Planning (CBTFP) [1], offered a parameterized feedback control law that generated safe trajectories between user-specified start and goal states in partially observable environments. The more recent evolution, the safety filter, represents an improved algorithm capable of handling additional constraints, such as ensuring safety during transient phases, while minimizing their impact on final trajectories.

To achieve this, we shift the focus from controlling individual trajectories to controlling distinction between safe and potentially unsafe belief states. Since distinction between safe and potentially unsafe trajectories can also be specified, we show how to synthesize a control strategy that ensures either objective while minimizing the frequency of unsafe distinctions between trajectories

We introduce a novel measurement device capable of monitoring the complete spatio-temporal evolution of single-photon quantum states, thereby detecting a broad spectrum of quantum hacking attacks targeting standard QKD protocols that utilize coherent states over optical fiber. Validated experimentally over an 80-meter fiber link, this all-pass quantum state monitor significantly enhances the security of practical QKD systems. Our findings demonstrate that even quiet fiber connections, previously thought to be safe, are susceptible to timing attacks utilizing timed coherent pulses; these attacks reduce the secure key distance to approximately 10 kilometers, aligning it with loss-tolerant bounds for phase-encoded QKD over lossy fiber. Additionally, we detail a widely applicable quantum hacking attack known as the Hermitian attack, which leverages the quantum state monitor's ability to measure the Hermitian part of the quantum state. This attack not only yields information about transmitted signals but also amplifies signals traversing quiet fiber, enabling remote eavesdropping without any signal detection. This phenomenon arises from the nonlinearity inherent in interacting a pumped single-photon detector with the field's quantum vacuum. Beyond QKD, this monitoring tool offers a general method for characterizing the quantum behavior of light fields in optical experiments involving weak coherent or single-photon sources. The functionality of the monitor is demonstrated through various experiments, and the associated technology is detailed in the supplementary material. The monitoring device is constructed by integrating a pumped single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) into a standard QKD test bench, equipped with a polarizing beam splitter (PBS) and two optical switches (OS) that alternate between signal and attack phases. By measuring the coincidence of the internal SPAD's clicks with an external detector, the system can determine both the arrival time and the complete spatio-temporal quantum state (wave packet shape) of incoming photons. This is achieved by analyzing the coincidence rate across different phases of delayed versions of the optical switch. Furthermore, the detection circuit can function as a standard QKD receiver by continuously rotating the phase of the basis measurement. The development of this monitor relied on open-source QKD software and off-the-shelf components, making it a practical solution for diagnosing first-order coherence and the wave packet shapes of experimental quantum states. Finally, we illustrate that extending the delay range of the optical switches allows the monitor to capture the spatio-temporal quantum behavior of photons over even longer distances.
