itate a fundamental shift in resource allocation strategies, as Base Stations (BSs) will integrate computational capabilities into the access layer to support computationally intensive tasks like augmented and virtual reality. This shift enables Offloading Assisted Computing (OAC), wherein mobile devices execute local computations or offload selected workloads to nearby access-point BSs. To optimize this paradigm, we introduce a joint optimization framework that addresses three specific questions: (i) Which tasks should be offloaded? (ii) How should uplink resources be allocated? and (iii) How can we jointly design task offloading and uplink resource allocation to maximize system performance? Focusing on latency-sensitive applications, our problem formulation aims to minimize end-to-end (E2E) latency while ensuring quality-of-service (QoS) constraints are met. Due to the integer nature of task allocation and the non-convexity of latency functions with respect to power and rate, solving these problems optimally is computationally prohibitive for large-scale systems. Consequently, we propose two sub-optimal algorithms with significantly lower computational complexity: (a) For question (i) and (ii), two iterative schemes are developed—one based on linearization and another as a closed-form solution. (b) For question (iii), two efficient algorithms are designed: one utilizes a closed-form rate allocation formula and the other an iterative approach. Simulation results demonstrate that the algorithms solving (iii) effectively enhance overall system performance, while those addressing (i) and (ii) quickly converge to a near-optimal solution. Furthermore, it is verified that all proposed algorithms consistently satisfy QoS constraints. End-to-end latency comparisons reveal that the closed-form algorithms incur less than 10% additional power and signaling overhead compared to optimal solutions, while the iterative algorithms result in less than 20% overhead. Additionally, it is observed that these sub-optimal algorithms achieve lower computational complexity than existing state-of-the-art methods.

The second focuses on derivative (DER) reachability, assessing how system trajectories respond to variations in the input. Both methods are extensively applied to optimal control problems involving quadratic objectives, which model a wide range of scenarios in control theory and physics. These problems can be solved efficiently using a unified algorithm that generates a family of linear difference equations; the specific instance relevant to a given system is identified by examining the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the resulting matrix. This matrix is consistently an orthogonal product of two symmetrizable matrices: one consistently positive definite and the other Hermitian. Furthermore, we establish eigenvalue bounds for the original system based on those of this factorized matrix. Each of the two matrices is directly linked to the original data, enabling the consistent computation of both upper and lower eigenvalue estimates. We demonstrate that the resulting condition number is invariably less than the condition number derived directly from the primary matrix. These findings hold significant potential for enhancing robustness in the analysis of IO and DER reachability. Additionally, we explore the broader implications of these results for matrix analysis and computational linear algebra. Specifically, we examine various algorithms for solving linear systems and invert matrices, showing that the conditional efficiency of these algorithms is improved when leveraging our eigenvalue bounds. Finally, we investigate the consistently superior performance of Givens rotation and the QR algorithm over the LU decomposition and Hessenberg-Schur algorithms in this context. These conclusions remain robust across all dynamical systems with quadratic objectives, including discrete-time and continuous-time linear quadratic regulators, minimum energy control, nonlinear spectral theory via the Evans function, and related areas.

In this model, waves are introduced via current injection through a patch of the boundary plane, causing magnetic field lines to oscillate like stretched rubber bands. This energy propagation occurs via Alfvén waves traveling along these magnetic field lines. The study compares scenarios where the global topology varies—from totally open to totally closed—while the local topology near the injecting patch remains consistent. When the background magnetic field is partially open, injected wave energy is confined to the field lines of the injecting patch and dissipates via resistivity. Conversely, in totally open or closed configurations, the energy spreads out, causing field lines to nearly perpendicularly cross the injecting patch plane before dissipating kinetically. These findings suggest that in interstellar clouds, both Alfvén waves traveling parallel to the local field and slow magnetosonic waves traveling perpendicularly can transport heat to small scales, where it dissipates to sustain the balance between cooling and heating. Additionally, the role of Hall currents in enabling slow magnetosonic waves is briefly mentioned. The proposed perpendicular cooling mechanism represents a novel concept, whereas parallel Alfvén wave transport has previously been extensively discussed in the context of turbulent magnetic energy cascades. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that injecting wave energy does not necessarily result in its accumulation on the injected field lines, even locally, unless global topological barriers prevent the energy from spreading.

The first tier models the network as an equilibrium problem within a relaxed state space, enhancing the master-slave structure of nonlinear systems. The second tier constructs a robust controller for the two-tier system by integrating the enhanced equilibrium problem with the original state-constrained problem, utilizing an augmented Lagrangian technique to handle constraints and a game-theoretic multi-agent approach to achieve robustness against modeling errors. The proposed two-tier equilibrium problem achieves superior performance compared to naive equilibrium strategies. The efficacy of this two-tier methodology is demonstrated through a seven-bus power network numerical case study. Ultimately, this work establishes a framework for centrally enhanced, robustly stable equilibrium in large-scale nonlinear networks subject to state constraints. These techniques are benchmarked against exact quantum simulation, optical full-neighbour tight-binding, and quantum electrodynamics on a lattice. Since multiple 2D projections can result from different 3D poses and lighting, decoupling orientation from pose instantiation allows the model to focus on inferring orientation more effectively. However, because multiple pose instances may produce identical projections given a certain orientation, this simplification can lead to performance degradation. This approach automatically generates a disjoint representation for each category and recovers virtual poses without the need for additional data. Ultimately, our method enables more efficient learning of pose-disjoint representations and improves pose estimation accuracy, even when combined with existing pose estimation techniques.

of a sample of size $N$ drawn from a Cauchy distribution. While this distribution involves two parameters—a location parameter $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and a scale parameter $\sigma > 0$—we will estimate them simultaneously by treating them as a unified complex parameter defined as $\gamma := \mu + i\sigma$. The resulting region will be a domain within the complex plane, and we will provide a simple, explicit formula to represent it as either a disc or a square. This approach builds upon the work of H.-D. Kim and M. Kim, who developed a similar method for the real parameter $\mu$. Our methodology relies on an inequality first published by G. Polya. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a real parameter $\mu$ and a complex parameter $\gamma$, the confidence intervals or regions originally derived by C. Cramer and H. Rubin remain valid. We begin with single-parameter inference before extending the discussion to joint inference. First, following Kim and Kim, we derive a confidence interval for $\mu$. Subsequently, using an inequality by G. Polya, we generalize this result to the Cauchy parameter $\gamma$. This yields a confidence region that can be depicted as a disc or a square in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. Our analysis indicates that the size of this region is approximately twice as large as those obtained using methods proposed by D. S. Gates, J. S. Marriot, and more recently by the authors of [11]. This approach offers an alternative to the techniques previously mentioned. Furthermore, as noted in [20], these methods are also applicable to other scale-location families, including the family of four-parameter distributions introduced by G. Galambos in [15]. This paper serves as a continuation of [21]. Keywords: Cauchy parameter, confidence region, inequality by G. Polya, joint confidence region, disc or square. This study identifies and characterizes the stellar flare emission mechanism responsible for ground-based audio sounds. By analyzing light and spectroscopic data from three flares on 10 Puppis (10 Pup), we determine that electron acceleration in intense magnetic fields produces hard X-ray emission, which is then scattered off interstellar hydrogen to generate UV photons ionizing ground-level air and creating acoustic sounds. This process drives the formation of radio bursts via the Electron Cyclotron Maser mechanism. Consequently, audio sounds recorded by ground-based instruments serve as proof that electron acceleration and magnetic field intensity are sufficient to trigger radio bursts observable by space-based observatories. We have developed an audio recorder for ground-based stellar flares and converted radio data into an audio format accessible to both professionals and amateurs. These findings enable the anticipated detection of white-crown flares that emit radio bursts above detection thresholds through ground-based audio recording. Such findings support the proposal of using ground-based audio sound as an indicator for the early detection of stellar flares and their emitted radio bursts. This approach holds significant potential for expanding the sample size of radio flares and conducting statistical studies on ionized stellar winds and magnetic fields. Furthermore, this method offers a pathway for predicting solar flares and associated space weather risks. We propose establishing a global network of ground-based audio recorders to early detect stellar and solar radio flares. This research also lays the foundation for future "radio astronomy" conducted through ground-based sound. As a supplementary initiative, we encourage the creation of a software interface designed to translate radio data into audio format. This study represents the inaugural proof-of-concept for early detection methods relying on ground-based audio sound. Keywords: Stars: Flares; Stars: Radio; Sun: Flares; Space Weather; Solar System.

While some works detected the ETPA signal by comparing the sample's transmission with that of a control experiencing single-photon absorption (SPA), the validity of this conclusion remains questionable. This is because the total absorption signal is merely a component of the joint wavefunction probability; other components, where neither photon is absorbed, can also contribute. To clarify these interactions, we introduce a comprehensive experimental framework that decomposes the absolute absorption signal into its constituent parts. Our experiments and numerical simulations indicate that non-ETPA contributions are more significant when overlaps are small. Finally, to validate the framework's applicability, we present experimental results obtained using a chi-two crystal. These findings offer novel insights into understanding the complete absorption signal and open new avenues for accurately experimentally distinguishing between SPA and ETPA contributions.

To extend this method, we investigate its applicability to graph states within multipartite quantum systems. Although graph states and Bell kernels are typically formulated using Paczyński's representation of Pauli groups, our analysis is conducted primarily in Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and the quantum group SU(2) framework, which is better suited for handling symmetry constraints. Our findings indicate that an all-versus-nothing proof of Bell nonlocality for graph states is generally unattainable; it is only possible under specific conditions regarding the graph's structure. Furthermore, we examine the connection between this type of proof and quantum packing problems. Since finding the maximum quantum packing is a NP-hard problem, we propose employing graph neural networks as a heuristic solution. We present several graph states for which Bell nonlocality can be proven using this approach, including the 3-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state, the 4-qubit cluster state, and the 5-qubit code state. Additionally, these selected nonlocal correlations enable self-testing for the mentioned quantum states. Finally, we highlight that implementing a deep convolutional neural network to address quantum packing can be efficiently accomplished in terms of quantum circuit depth. However, the necessary classical computational resources for training the network remain substantial. Consequently, leveraging transfer learning is suggested as a viable strategy to overcome this obstacle.

Question marks constitute the most prevalent punctuation mark in English. Although prior linguistic analyses have largely overlooked them, this note initiates an information-theoretic examination of their function. We observe that the majority of occurrences fall into three categories: introductions, continuations, and terminations. Our primary contribution is demonstrating that question marks are not redundant; rather, they increase the entropy of both incoming and outgoing contexts. We validate these claims empirically and illustrate their practical utility by applying them to various string processing tasks. Specifically, we show that question marks facilitate faster compression, enable quicker parsing, and assist in disambiguating entity mentions. By integrating structural, syntactic, and semantic features, we achieve the highest accuracy reported to date for detecting entity mentions containing question marks. Additionally, we demonstrate superior performance in entity linking and entity alignment compared to state-of-the-art methods, even when trained on data excluding questions. We attribute this success to the fact that existing approaches struggle to handle questions effectively. To support future research, we have made the annotated dataset used in this study publicly available. This data was collected by parsing Wikipedia off-disk snapshots and extracting relevant sections from each page. The dataset can be accessed at: http://www.csl.sri.com/~bhagwan/wikiquot/.

Achieving this requires two main components: a fault detection module to identify errors and a fail-safe mechanism to maintain safety despite those errors. While the detection module is well-documented, literature on the fail-safe mechanism remains scarce. This paper introduces and validates a systematic approach to developing such mechanisms within automotive contexts. A key contribution is the utilization of SOTIF (Safety Of The Intelligent Vehicle) to mitigate functional misuse and expectation violation risks. The proposed fail-safe mechanism allows the vehicle to continue operation by switching to human control while finding a secure location off the road. Validation occurs through a fault injection campaign combining hardware-in-the-loop simulations with real-world driving. Results indicate that the fail-safe mechanism successfully manages all analyzed risks, with only one false positive and no false negatives. Furthermore, activating the mechanism takes less than two seconds in every instance, ensuring sufficient reaction time. Finally, the validation process itself is suggested as a template for assessing similar system designs. Overall, the authors believe that their methodology significantly advances the state of the art in designing fault-tolerant systems.

The Leibniz Institute for Information Technology and Science (LIT) has signaled its preference for the principle of bivalence and classical first-order logic (FOL). While standard first-order logic relies on bivalence, it fails to accommodate alternative truth principles. We demonstrate that mFOL captures the essential features of known bivalence by proving that it is equivalent to classical FOL augmented with the axiom stating that every sentence is known to be either true or false. arsity, which arises when users fail to rate every item, and the Vondran-Tulczyowicz theorem indicates that alogarithmic number of ratings per item are necessary to precisely recover user preferences. This paper examines the sparsity problem within the context of private recommendation systems, where items possess either public or secret values relative to the system. Specifically, we focus on scenarios where the system possesses public values that correlate with user ratings. Assuming these public values are strictly public—meaning no partial information about unrated items is revealed to the user—we demonstrate that the fundamental lower bound on the number of required ratings remains unchanged compared to cases without public values. Furthermore, we introduce ValPublic, the first recommendation framework that achieves performance comparable to the optimal non-private case. ValPublic is the first to exploit public values to enhance space efficiency and their correlation with user ratings without compromising privacy. In contrast, when values are secret—sharing no correlation with user ratings—we show that the lower bound on ratings does not degrade. However, in this secret valuation scenario, providing an efficient private recommendation system is impossible, and we establish the precise trade-off between space efficiency and computational complexity. Finally, our lower bounds are tight, and ValPublic performs nearly optimally in terms of both space and computation efficiency. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets confirm that these algorithms achieve near-optimal performance.

Specifically, we examine structural characteristics of $(1,1)$-configurations in graphs that lack a perfect matching, with an emphasis on the case where $k$ is an odd integer. We demonstrate that graphs devoid of $(1,1)$-configurations can be transformed into those possessing a perfect matching through the addition of edges. Additionally, we analyze the minimum cardinality of fractional $(1,1)$-configurations in graphs without a perfect matching, deriving related insights for unimodular matrices. To facilitate easy development on these hardware accelerators, compilers translate P4 code into various underlying hardware architectures. One prominent example is the MXIA, an xIA-based SDA supported by an open-source compiler that maps P4 programs directly to a low-level hardware abstraction. Due to the significant performance variations between different xIA implementations, understanding the operational details of the MXIA is crucial for writing efficient P4 code. Currently, the only available resource is a 120-page technical report featuring a limited online search. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a novel software model of the MXIA and developing a corresponding P4 simulator. Beyond enabling accurate P4 code testing during development, this simulator also serves an educational purpose: it allows students to grasp the complex inner workings of the xIA family through a straightforward software-based approach. The presentation will highlight the problems related to MXIA's under-documentation and how this simulator resolves it. Additionally, it will explain the authors' experience integrating the MXIA simulator into the P4 flow-based compiler stack and demonstrate how it enhances both development and teaching xIA-based systems. Finally, the audience will be invited to explore the simulator interactively. This talk will briefly review the simulator's features and can be delivered in various formats depending on the time allocated and the target audience.

The ethical deployment of deep learning is significantly hindered by three primary obstacles: communication limitations, data privacy concerns, and bias. This paper proposes a unified framework incorporating three novel algorithms to simultaneously address these issues and explore their interdependencies. Experiments across adult classification and longitudinal dimensionality reduction tasks demonstrate that federated learning can train high-quality models with minimal data privacy risks on extensive datasets. Additionally, we introduce a new backpropagation-based method that achieves near-optimal accuracy and bias reduction while substantially decreasing computation time compared to existing approaches. Finally, we examine interactions between ethical principles and federated learning, as well as backdoor attacks, highlighting vulnerabilities in current solutions. The goal is to create models that capture diverse data subgroups without requiring the exchange of raw inputs, while simultaneously optimizing two critical metrics: representation size and communication overhead. Achieving low communication requires minimizing frequency, duration, and bandwidth. To address this, we propose using quantized models instead of full-precision ones. By analyzing the dynamics, we identify bounds for the system's escape age. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system exhibits quasi-periodic and chaotic behaviors, with parameters showing strong sensitivity influencing the system's dynamics. Collectively, these results provide comprehensive numerical evidence regarding the system's dynamics, suggesting potential applications in stochastic search and optimization within complex, rugged landscapes. These findings complement our previous work on analogous two-dimensional systems, for which analytical solutions exist. This review is particularly pertinent today, as planet formation emerges as a consequence of SF, offering a fresh perspective on the broader inquiry into the origin of life in the universe. The structure of the paper is as follows: Section 2 outlines the current status of SF theory; Section 3 discusses key observational findings related to SF; and Section 4 presents our conclusions.

Observational data confirms that star formation occurs within dense molecular cloud cores, specifically within isolated over-densities that collapse under gravity to create a protostar. However, the mechanisms triggering this collapse remain unclear. To address this, theory posits that SF results from the instability of these dense cores, predicting a characteristic "linear branching" pattern in star-forming regions. Yet, observations reveal that "fragmenting branching" is more prevalent. This happens because the instabilities arising from turbulent pressure are non-linear, driven by supersonic turbulence prevalent in molecular clouds. Consequently, SF is better modeled as a complex fluid-dynamic process, a revelation that has significantly altered theoretical frameworks. Current theories utilize complex simulations incorporating complex N-body systems, magnetohydrodynamics, and radiative hydrodynamics to understand SF and the early evolution of star-forming regions. These simulations demonstrate that a single star cluster can originate from a single dense core, spanning a vast scale from approximately 10 parsecs. Furthermore, the theory indicates that star formation is fundamentally a turbulent process, allowing for the estimation of the total energy invested in creating stars, which is roughly 1000 times greater than the gravitational energy released by the stars themselves. A pivotal aspect triggered by this turbulence is magnetic field amplification via the dynamo effect, a mechanism capable of influencing the galactic evolution of star-forming regions. Therefore, both SF theory and observational data have undergone substantial changes in their development, offering a new perspective on how stars form, evolve, and potentially give rise to life.

Research shows that $t_D$ is much longer than both $t_{ff}$ and $t_0$. This allows us to divide the evolution of star-forming regions into three phases. Additionally, our findings explain why inelastic light scattering from the surface of a solid exhibits a distinct peak at low wave vectors compared to the high-$q$ peak; this occurs because atomic displacements increase as one approaches the surface. Our findings indicate that multi-objective optimization does not consistently yield high diversity, multimodal optimization generates solutions with superior fitness, and quality diversity remains unaffected by genetic neutrality while producing the most diverse outcomes. Furthermore, employing multi-objective optimization under specific parameter configurations can achieve results comparable to those of quality diversity. Multi-objective optimization seeks non-dominated solutions that cannot be surpassed in all objectives without compromising others. Conversely, quality diversity aims to discover solutions exhibiting unique behaviors alongside high quality. Although both approaches generate multiple solutions, they utilize distinct fitness evaluations: multi-objective optimization relies on objective values, whereas quality diversity uses a composite of qualities and uniqueness. This paper demonstrates that applying multi-objective optimization with unsupervised uniqueness metrics yields results comparable to or better than quality diversity, particularly when uniqueness metrics are well-designed. Furthermore, multi-objective optimization effectively handles genetic neutrality better than quality diversity, offering faster discovery of varied high-quality solutions. Consequently, multi-objective optimization presents a viable alternative to quality diversity, maintaining simplicity by relying solely on automatic fitness functions.

Multiple solutions often exist to a problem, yet they may fail to generalize to new instances. To address this, various algorithms have been developed to discover multiple solutions, including multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity. These methods produce distinct solution sets characterized by differing fitness components: objective values, a fitness score, and a combination of fitness and uniqueness, respectively. This study compares the solution sets generated by these three approaches to determine which algorithm yields the best results. Our results show that quality diversity discovers the highest quantity of unique solutions, multimodal optimization yields the superior fitness, and multi-objective optimization achieves the greatest uniqueness. Moreover, an empirical analysis reveals that an ideal uniqueness metric for multi-objective optimization should be supervised, linearly independent of fitness, and capture significant variations to ensure generalizability.

While traditional versions demand even numbers of agents, generalizing this to odd numbers or unequal team sizes creates significant challenges. Specifically, agents cannot form teams of two if the total count is odd, and determining stable matchings for other team sizes is non-trivial. This paper addresses the case where all team sizes equal two, even for an odd number of agents. We prove that a stable matching always exists under these conditions and present an $O(n^3)$-time algorithm to find one. This represents a substantial improvement over the previously best known $O(n^5)$-time approach by Manlove and McDermott \cite{manlove2020}. Furthermore, our method is more efficient than solving the problem by reducing it to instances with even agents; a naive reduction to the nearest even number incurs a penalty of at least a factor of four. Finally, we investigate stable matchings for team size three. We demonstrate that while stable matchings exist when all sizes are three, they do not necessarily exist in a mixed scenario with teams of sizes two and three. Analysis reveals that existence depends on the absence of specific "impairements." Determining existence can be done in polynomial time for pure size three instances but is NP-hard for the mixed case. This distinguishes team formulations from individual roommate problems, highlighting the impact of team sizing assumptions on existence. We also examine other team sizes, confirming existence for size three and analyzing the NP-hard complexities that arise with size four. The individual case with team size two remains an open question. Across various problems and their team-based variants, our findings indicate that team sizing assumptions significantly influence both existence and computational complexity.

This study investigates whether quantum sensors can enhance their readout sensitivity beyond the shot noise limit by exploiting quantum correlations within photon number superposition states. Our findings indicate that for general multimode coherent states, this readout noise reduction is achievable. Consequently, multimode coherent states represent an optimal choice for enhancing quantum sensor sensitivity at the readout stage. We further analyze how temporal correlations influence the collective squeezing required for multimode coherent states and propose a simple state preparation method to generate them. Finally, we demonstrate that multimode coherent states can significantly improve the readout sensitivity of two essential quantum sensors: a common-mode optomechanical nanomechanical sensor and an optically readout strontium atomic clock. Specifically, the readout sensitivity of the optomechanical nanomechanical sensor can be enhanced by approximately three times, while the short-term frequency stability of the strontium atomic clock can be improved by a factor of 1.15. These results suggest that multimode coherent states have substantial potential to advance quantum sensing applications. Furthermore, multimode coherent states can be prepared through either quantum or classical correlations, offering new insights into the role of quantum correlations in quantum metrology. Classical-correlated multimode coherent states are especially promising, as they overcome the need to maintain quantum correlations during the evolution from preparation to measurement, a process that is often fragile and susceptible to decoherence. Therefore, classical-correlated multimode coherent states are expected to serve as a valuable resource for quantum metrology.

Results indicate that extreme model sizes push architectures toward simplified search spaces, yielding more deterministic optimal regions, whereas mid-range sizes (characteristic of many vision models) generate more stochastic optimal regions. This study investigates how orbital phase and distance relative to the central star currently limit the minimum observable planet parameters using coronagraphs and direct laser comb interferometers. By employing reduced-order modeling, we demonstrate that the closest approach distance ($r_{app}$) creates starlight speckle noise indistinguishable from planet light, resulting in rapidly varying contrast performance. Consequently, there exists an observational "dead zone" of radius $\sim 2.5 \lambda/D$ around the star where no orbit is optimal for finding Earth-mass planets at a given orbit period ($P_{orb}$). The size and location of this dead zone shift based on $P_{app}$, the angle between the star-planet vector and the line of sight. To observe an Earth-mass planet at $P_{orb}=1$ year around a sun-like star from 10 pc away, the initial conditions must fall outside this dead zone. Furthermore, we propose three strategies to mitigate dead zone effects: (1) utilizing planets with longer $P_{orb}$ to increase $r_{app}$ and elevate the detectable mass; (2) conducting observations at $P_{orb}/4$ or $3P_{app}/4$ to target phases with larger star-planet angular separations; and (3) continuously tracking orbital phases to gather data across multiple quarters, thereby averaging out dead zone influences. These reduced-order models offer a computationally efficient method for optimizing the initial conditions of high-contrast planet searches. Additionally, we extend this approach to determine optimal integration times for comb-spectrograph observations of exoplanets.

We demonstrate that logarithmic constraint systems admit multiple distinct yet physically equivalent forms, providing a clear and practical guide for selecting the most suitable representation in various contexts. Furthermore, we clarify the connection to entropic constraints. Most critically, we show that these forms establish a unique correspondence with specific logarithmic holonomies, showing that non-holonomic constraints cannot be expressed in terms of holonomies. Finally, we examine several important applications, including CO2 molecules, Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transitions, anyons, quantum field theory, black holes, cosmic strings, entropy, and information theory. Notably, physical phases featuring a non-vanishing entropic anomaly represent thermodynamic systems governed by logarithmic constraint systems, with the entropic anomaly serving as a measure of their degree; this phenomenon has previously been identified only in two dimensions. Any logarithmic constraint system can be transformed into a standard form that remains independent of choices regarding representations, physical contexts, or specific applications. Although quantum systems cannot utilize non-holonomic constraints, our analysis reveals that numerous systems previously believed to rely on them actually require a different type: logarithmic constraints. This work clarifies the distinctions between these two logarithmic constraint systems and offering guidance for implementing them. We emphasize that choosing between them is not arbitrary, as the alternative form incorporates non-trivial long-range interactions with specific physical significance. We illustrate this significance through anyons, showing how to derive their braiding properties from logarithmic constraint systems. Anyons represent two-dimensional quantum statistical mechanical systems, distinct from planar spin systems, that exhibit non-trivial logarithmic holonomies within their algebra of observables, corresponding to non-trivial logarithmic constraint systems. In contrast, CO2 molecules, which represent three-dimensional physical systems relying on genuine logarithmic constraints, provide a three-dimensional physical model of logarithmic holonomies and non-trivial long-range interactions. These findings extend to solvable logarithmic conformal field theories, offering new physical interpretations for them. We conclude that thermodynamic phases characterized by non-vanishing entropic anomalies are correctly described by logarithmic constraint systems, a phenomenon previously observed only in two dimensions. This research establishes for the first time the existence of physical systems in three and higher dimensions governed by logarithmic constraint systems, confirming that such systems are not limited to lower-dimensional cases. This represents significant new solvable models for understanding quantum statistical mechanical and thermodynamic phases in three and higher dimensions.

To improve the efficacy of deep neural networks (DNNs) within Internet of Things (IoT) environments, this study introduces a novel compression technique called bidirectional progressive pruning training (BiP2). Since forward inference and backward gradient calculations in DNN training involve redundant operations, this work examines pruning methods that leverage these redundancies. The proposed approach consists of two phases: initially, forward and backward pass pruning separately iteratively prune neurons exhibiting redundant activity during forward and backward passes, respectively, while training a new network from scratch. Subsequently, bidirectional progressive pruning training jointly and progressively prune neurons based on both forward and backward features. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior compression ratios and maintains performance comparable to unpruned models. To further enhance compression, the study proposes a binary neuron encoding scheme that represents neuron weights using 1-bit precision. Evaluations demonstrate that binary neuron encoding can compress weights by approximately 4 times without significantly impacting overall network performance. Finally, the proposed methods were implemented and tested on an actual IoT edge device, the Raspberry Pi 4, to validate their effectiveness in reducing training time and memory consumption. The experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed techniques can effectively train deep neural networks on Raspberry Pis. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/kiyotaka-iitaka/iot-edge-deep-neural-network-pruning.

The hadronic equation of state is particularly sensitive to the presence of hybrid baryons, which carry quantum numbers unavailable to ordinary baryons. These hybrid states emerge in regions where one or more chiral condensates are partially or fully broken. This study examines the properties of hybrid mesons and octet-antioctet scalar, vector, and pseudoscalar particles using the Chiral Solitary Model (CSM). Our calculations demonstrate that these hybrid states appear at energies and densities comparable to those of kaon condensation. The emergence of hybrid particles—carrying quantum numbers unlike those of standard particles—could signal a partially or fully restored chiral symmetry in the vacuum, offering critical insights into strong interaction dynamics at high energies. Prior theoretical investigations have identified these particles at energies exceeding several GeV. However, in the context of QCD vacuum modification under extreme temperature or density, such as inside neutron stars, hybrid particles may arise at significantly lower energy scales. Specifically, we anticipate that scalar, vector, and pseudoscalar particles with isospin $I=1$ could develop decay channels into two photons at densities comparable to the onset of kaon condensation. Consequently, high-energy cosmic neutrinos interacting with bulk matter in neutron stars or accretion disks surrounding neutron stars and black holes could produce photons with energies around a few MeV, potentially detectable by next-generation X-ray telescopes such as STIX on STIX, eXTP, or APEX on the International Space Station.

These interactions are complex and context-dependent, making them difficult to capture in simple terms. However, leveraging principles from系统工程 (systems engineering) allows for a more accurate depiction of the intricately intertwined states within host-virus interactions. To explore this, we introduce the concept of entropy as a metric for cellular state complexity. As viral infection intensifies, cell metabolism shifts toward cell death, resulting in negative entropy. By applying control theory, we examine the stability of cellular systems alongside invading entities. We illustrate that both cells and viruses function as two distinct parts of an integrated system governed by negative feedback mechanisms. Consequently, the interaction between a cell and an invading virus increases the overall complexity and stability threshold of the system. Paradoxically, despite this heightened complexity, the net change in the total entropy of the combined system remains negative. Paradoxically, this negative entropy change correlates with the emergence of invasive behaviors in both partners. Drawing on these insights, we discuss the potential for engineering new antiviral drugs and cancer therapies. Furthermore, we note that our model's ability to interpret entropy change offers a foundation for developing new methodologies to combat infectious diseases. Finally, while our discussion has focused on invasive viruses and cancer, the underlying mechanisms extend to other scenarios involving cellular interaction, invasion, and physical interactions between matter and life. Additionally, our framework suggests new directions for antimicrobial product design and bio-material engineering. More broadly, the entropy change mechanism proposed here contributes to deepening our fundamental understanding of universal principles. Specifically, it elucidates how interactions between two entities can elevate system complexity while driving the universe toward lower entropy, thereby addressing the question of why the universe exhibits complexity despite trending toward lower entropy. We hope this work inspires future interdisciplinary endeavors.

This study aims to clarify their morphology by analyzing the 12 CO(J=1-0) and 13 CO(J=1-0) molecular gas maps of 18 such galaxies, alongside their Hubble images and optical emission line data. Classical arped disks exhibit a wide range of ionized gas distributions, but their molecular and atomic gases consistently align with optical imaging. We propose that classical arped disks result from external interactions with dark matter halos, whereas lopsided disks are formed by internal secular evolution. Furthermore, nearly all classical arped disks display optical isophotal boxy/diamond-shaped structures, suggesting that optical boxy bulges are primary products of galaxy mergers. Given that modern codebases have evolved to include abundant textual data, researchers have begun treating commit histories as first-class representations of developer activity. In this framework, dark energy arises from quantum zero-point fluctuations within a finite space governed by discrete physics, while dark matter emerges from a gravitational confinement mechanism. This framework reveals the potential for strong coupling between neutral atoms and photonic crystal cavities, offering new avenues for investigating photonic crystal physics, developing related technologies, and applying these systems in advanced quantum technology contexts.

The interaction between neutral atoms and optical fields is fundamentally altered when confined in photonic crystals due to their unique interaction mechanisms. While many approaches achieve sample efficiency by designing imitation algorithms that depend solely on online data from a stationary expert policy, most such methods struggle when the target environment differs from the expert's. We introduce a novel framework that transforms offline imitation learning into a standard supervised learning problem, enabling the direct learning of desired actions within a novel environment. This is accomplished by training a model on online trajectories generated by the target environment using a specific imitation loss, followed by updating this model with expert demonstrations using online updating techniques. This approach represents the first solution to offline imitation learning in settings where offline data cannot assume a stationary distribution. Although the method remains online, it utilizes significantly more data than previous solutions. Furthermore, we apply this approach to offline option discovery, and experimental results on standard benchmarks demonstrate that it surpasses prior methods. Additionally, the method recovers near-optimal expert policies using approximately 100 times less data than other offline imitation learning approaches.

Motivated by the emerging need to analyze high-dimensional data, this work examines statistical learning in multi-dimensional vector spaces. Given the growing importance of multidimensional data in modern computing, this research holds significant practical value.

The method is based on the observation that distinct process states can be characterized by their frequency distribution over time. Since prior research has demonstrated that spectral analysis effectively identifies distinct components within a time series, we extend the existing spectral approach for detecting distinct components. Specifically, we apply spectral analysis to the estimated forward and backward probabilities of HMMs, followed by the identification of distinct components using HMMs. Consequently, the proposed method decomposes the original time series into sub-series, each representing a distinct state. By calculating the statistical distance between these sub-series, the method distinguishes between in-control and out-of-control states. Consequently, an anomaly is defined as the presence of the out-of-control state. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through simulations using various spectral analysis techniques, with findings showing that the proposed method outperforms existing anomaly detection techniques. Furthermore, the method's reliability is validated across three real-world datasets: monitoring equipment vibrations, air quality measurements, and medical imaging data. In all cases, anomalies were successfully detected with high precision, confirming the method's effectiveness. Additionally, the results indicate that the algorithm is computationally efficient. Therefore, this approach is well-suited for monitoring and anomaly detection in critical processes. Finally, the method is anticipated to be applicable in various other contexts. The algorithm is implemented in R and Java, and the source code is publicly available. The process involves encoding each input modality into a mode-specific embedding, concatenating these embeddings, and then passing the result through a classifier to predict identity (or reject). A key advantage of this architecture is its straightforward interpretability, as the contribution of each modality to the final decision is explicit. However, our primary objective is to resolve issues related to insufficient and redundant information. To achieve this, we introduce two novel modules: Spatial Information Filtering (SIF) and Redundancy Reduction (RRED). The SIF module enhances visual data by eliminating irrelevant details through a cropping mechanism that selects non-overlapping regions, while the RRED module mitigates redundancy by applying channel-wise attention across two networks of differing aspect ratios. Experiments were conducted on two datasets: MediaEval Person Verification 2019 and MediaEval Person Re-Identification 2020. Using only appearance inputs with SIF+rED models achieved mode-averaged F1 scores of 0.746 and 0.706 on the training and validation sets, respectively. Including profile inputs further improved mode-averaged F1 scores to 0.773 and 0.731 for the training and validation sets. In contrast, other recent methods yielded lower scores across all datasets. Additionally, we analyzed false positives and false negatives from the validation set across three categories: similar individuals, different individuals, and unknown persons. Results indicate that while the model performs well with high-F1 images from both datasets, it struggles to distinguish between similar people in the profile modality. To address this, we tested the effect of cropping the profile modality; however, due to varying degrees of redundancy in different images, simply cropping did not consistently improve performance. Furthermore, we observed that increasing the number of channels in the encoder did not yield better outcomes, suggesting that the current model may already be near-optimal given the current data. Finally, we compared input formats, finding that while raw inputs resulted in lower performance, face-cropped and face-detected inputs performed significantly better. This highlights the critical role of visual data quality in multimodal person verification. Overall, we demonstrated that multimodal person verification is effective and that our proposed model outperforms other recent approaches. We believe these findings offer valuable insights into addressing information redundancy within multimodal systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/aryaprasad/MPV_model.

Recently, two promising approaches have emerged to address this problem: Differential Synoptic Mechanisms (DSM) and Differentially Constrained Optimization (DCO). Although fully private solutions exist within these frameworks, their practical application is often hindered by complex, difficult-to-solve private algorithms that fail to match the tractability of non-private alternatives. This paper introduces a novel methodology, Differentially Lagrangian Optimization with Randomized Rounding and Perturbation (DLO-RRP), which integrates two recently proposed private techniques—randomized rounding/dual perturbation and the Lagrangian relaxation framework. We demonstrate that DSM, DCO, and DLO-RRP are fundamentally interconnected, allowing for meaningful cross-pollination of privately executable methods. Specifically, DLO-RRP unifies recent advancements in private processing to produce an entirely private algorithm on one front, while simultaneously enhancing its data utility and computational efficiency on the other. This study investigates the interrelated nature of gas emission substructures in protoplanetary disks using hydrodynamical simulations. We applied this technique to analyze gas emission features in well-modeled disks (ALMA-J2031 and ALMA-ApEODS-D17), deriving morphological parameters for subtending radius, arc fraction, and peak width. To advance this initiative, we must develop robust theoretical and cosmological tools capable of addressing fundamental questions, such as the initial conditions of the Universe. In this study, we demonstrate that no singular trajectory exists within the space of inflationary cosmologies that can be derived from a consistent theory of quantum gravity. This study investigates the mechanisms of temperature-induced damage and degradation at the GaN-sapphire interface. Specifically, we analyzed how compressive stress releases at misfit dislocations and defects release oxygen from the interface into the GaN bulk, a process that impairs subsequent device performance. These findings are supported by density functional theory calculations and corroborated by previous experimental data. By enhancing template quality through our proposed strategies, the operational temperature limit for GaN-based devices on sapphire substrates can be significantly raised. By approximately one order of magnitude, this improvement enables the integration of fully functional GaN circuits into automotive headlamp systems. The general principles of temperature-limited interface stability in nitride materials may also have broader implications for other technological applications.

The increasing demand for efficient and reliable light sources has made temperature stability a critical factor in GaN technology. This work examines temperature-limited damage and degradation occurring at the GaN-sapphire interface and within the template. Compressive stress release at misfit dislocations and defects facilitates the diffusion of oxygen from the sapphire substrate into the GaN buffer layer using a recently proposed model. Such temperature-induced damage compromises the template quality and undermines the performance of future devices. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we identified unstable interface configurations that facilitate damage accumulation in both the interface and the buffer layer. We demonstrate that template reliability can be significantly improved by either releasing embedded gases or shifting dislocations during manufacturing. This strategy enables the development of fully functional GaN-based automotive headlamp circuits, which must withstand temperatures up to approximately 150°C. Additionally, we estimate that temperature-limited damage in sapphire-based templates currently restricts the maximum functionality of automotive headlamps. Finally, the principle of material stability in nitride materials under high temperature and pressure conditions is broadly applicable to various technological applications.

However, the inherent complexity and uncertainty within natural language processing present substantial hurdles for vanilla deep reinforcement learning. Consequently, integrating prior knowledge has become essential. Although existing approaches attempt to incorporate prior information into deep reinforcement learning, current methods are limited to processing only one type of data feature. In contrast, KYC compliance demands the processing of multiple data types, including text, images, and decision trees. Resolving this challenge is vital for developing more user-friendly and cost-effective compliance systems. Therefore, there is a critical need for a novel deep reinforcement learning technique capable of incorporating various types of prior information to address KYC challenges. This paper presents such a solution, presenting a deep reinforcement learning framework that successfully learns from multiple data sources.

KGE) offers promising opportunities for modeling dynamic knowledge. However, this domain remains underexplored, with only a few recent studies addressing time-aware knowledge graph embedding. Existing approaches generally fall into two categories: learning time-aware embeddings for entities and relations, or modeling time-aware relationships between entities. Current methods typically assign a single time-sensitive embedding to each entity, rendering them unsuitable for time-varying entity embeddings. Additionally, these approaches rely on time interpolation, which may not be effective when time-series data is sparse. To address these limitations, we introduce TimeKE, a novel sparsity-aware time-aware KGE model. We also investigate two strategies for time sensitivity: global vs. local and additive vs. multiplicative component interactions. Extensive experiments across various time-sensitive knowledge graphs, utilizing both held-out time instances and time-interval testing sets, demonstrate that TimeKE substantially surpasses current state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, our analyses of time-series split and time-interval split validation datasets, alongside ablation studies, reinforce the significance of our proposed improvements. Specifically, we highlight that the additive component interaction method yields superior results compared to the multiplicative variant.

Long-term temporal knowledge graph embedding aims to predict time-varying relationships within knowledge graphs. While additive and multiplicative convolutional methods have been widely adopted, the component interaction between time and graph structure remains unexplored. Based on these observations, we developed the component convolution network (CCN), the first model to address this gap by enabling interaction between time dimensions and graph structures. Extensive experiments across multiple time-long knowledge graphs validate the CCN's superior performance over popular additive and multiplicative convolutional methods. The source code is available at:  Our findings also suggest that the order of convolution operations significantly impacts model performance.

Existing time-aware knowledge graph embedding models typically employ time convolution to capture time-series patterns, yet they fail to model long-term dependencies, limiting their performance on distant time queries. To resolve this issue, we propose DC-LSTM, an innovative model that utilizes a dual-component convolutional long short-term memory network to capture both local and global time dependencies. Our experiments reveal that Dual Component LSTM substantially outperforms models relying solely on time convolution. We implement a model for the heavy quark loop contribution and determine the gluon propagation contribution using a phenomenological approach. Gluon propagation is examined through a phenomenological running coupling concept within a bulk medium, evaluated via the strong $\alpha_s$ in the in-medium state of heavy quarkonia. By incorporating all relevant contributions, we examine spectral properties and decay widths of $\psi(2S)$, $J/\psi$, and $\Upsilon(2S)$ as functions of temperature to compare with LHCb measurements. Additionally, we assess the reliability of our $\psi(2S)$ decay width predictions by comparing them with PROSA predictions under temperature-dependent conditions. Finally, our findings are discussed in the context of temperature-dependent potential models regarding quarkonium suppression observed at the LHC. These results indicate that, within the temperature range applicable to LHC experiments, our predictions for spectral properties and decay widths of quarkonium states are reasonable and reliable. Furthermore, we highlight the necessity of calculating the gluon propagation contribution in a medium, as it plays a critical role in determining both spectral properties and decay widths of quarkonium states at finite temperatures. This work advances our understanding of the mechanism governing quarkonium survival and provides crucial insights into the characteristics of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP). Specifically, our findings suggest a lower bound for the viscosity-to-entropy density ratio of the QGP. To ensure reliable lower bound estimates for this ratio, it is essential to refine our understanding of gluon propagation within a QGP medium. These findings may also offer valuable insights for analyzing astronomical objects containing quark matter. Finally, we address the temperature range relevant to LHC experiments in our conclusions.

While current document-grounded systems achieve high performance by designating a single document as a complete knowledge source—limiting their applicability to controlled environments—this focus on solitary documents restricts their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. We introduce KGQA-REtrieval-QA, a three-stage retrieval-based framework that integrates knowledge graphs to answer open-domain questions without relying on any knowledge graph alignment tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even with limited access to six entity-mention links, our approach retains only minimal knowledge about entity properties, relations, and events, yet remains highly effective in generating accurate responses. While programmatic prompts offer a more flexible and composable alternative, generating effective ones remains difficult because current models struggle to grasp their syntax effectively. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging the implicit control flow inherent in programmatic prompts to teach the model this syntax. Specifically, we design loss functions that manipulate the model's attention patterns to highlight prompt syntax structures. By focusing attention on relevant parts of the prompt, the model learns to interpret the syntax more effectively, resulting in significant performance gains. Consequently, this work demonstrates that shaping a model's attention through syntax control flow can effectively teach it grammar, thereby boosting its generalization capabilities. while existing methods for analyzing large-scale networks rely on sampling, they largely disregard the network's topology. Specifically, current sampling techniques treat vertices as random or adopt strategies optimized for uniform random graphs, rendering them suboptimal for topological graphs. Furthermore, the randomized approaches that do account for topology suffer from theoretical flaws, creating a gap between their promised performance and actual results. This work revisits graph cut functions to derive optimal cut values for linear extension sampling of directed acyclic graphs. We demonstrate that the leading term of the asymptotic cut value is driven by the graph's degree sequence rather than its topology, with only a second-order term capturing topological influence. Consequently, we propose a novel sampling algorithm with guaranteed asymptotic performance, where the leading term of the cut error depends exclusively on the second moments of the degree sequence alongside novel concentration inequalities for sum-of-functions on acyclic graphs. For graphs with bounded out-degrees, this yields sample sizes independent of the number of vertices. These methods are particularly well-suited for digraphs with small out-degrees, such as those found in dependency graphs. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world networks confirm the optimality of our sampling algorithm and its superior efficacy for graphs where topology significantly impacts cut values. In contrast, for general graphs, our method performs comparably to state-of-the-art sampling algorithms. Our GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/dsengupta0/linear-extension-sampling. Finally, we introduce the open-source dataset $\mathsf{LibGara}$, accessible at https://github.com/dsengupta0/LibGara, which contains over 1,500 large-scale directed acyclic graphs. Code for reproducing experimental results is included within this repository. Our results are optimized for linear extension sampling, defined as the order in which a vertex's ancestors are visited. This sampling scheme is widely adopted across mathematics, computer science, and operations research, including applications such as analyzing maximum weight antichains for the Lipschitz-Kotzig problem, estimating the size of the largest antichain, and computing the length of the longest path. Our approach extends naturally to other graph linear orderings and may be adaptable for other applications.

Title: Characterizing Unidirectionality in Microcavity Lasers Using Robust Measures of Shannon Entropy

Abstract: This study addresses two primary issues: finding a generalized way to characterize unidirectionality and revealing complex structures within microcavity emission profiles. To achieve this, we utilize two complementary definitions of Shannon entropy: one derived from semi-marginal probability distributions in Cartesian coordinates and the other from far-field distributions in polar coordinates. These measures effectively quantify emission structures in microcavity lasers with varying degrees of multimodality. Notably, both methods yield consistent results, demonstrating that this approach can robustly characterize not only fundamental transverse modes but also higher-order modes and their linear combinations. This characterization method is broadly applicable to any microcavity system involving a competition between optical confinement effects and linear propagation. To illustrate the method's utility, we applied it to explain strikingly nontrivial internal structures within seemingly unimodal steady-state emission profiles of a distributed Bragg reflector microdisk cavity

Large deviations characterize rare events and constitute a significant area of modern probability theory. Specifically, this study analyzes a rare event where solar plasma and magnetic field measurements intersect with coronal mass ejection (CME) material in the inner heliosphere, creating an ideal dataset for investigating CME evolution under nearly identical physical conditions. Measurements from the FPI and RM instruments are compared against in-situ models of CME evolution, focusing on both isotropic and anisotropic scenarios, with theoretical predictions validated against other published observations. Within the CME sheath, power spectral density (PSD) of plasma and magnetic field fluctuations is approximated by a power law across the studied frequency range, yielding a slope of roughly $-5.3$ for plasma and $-2.8$ for magnetic fields. These slopes indicate that fluctuations at sub-ion scales in the CME sheath are more intense and more frequent than those typically found in the CME sheath or at solar scales. Furthermore, the CME sheath exhibits more significant and complex small-scale fluctuations in both plasma and magnetic fields compared to the CME body or the corona. Notably, the CME sheath displays steeper small-scale slopes and more complex behavior than the CME body, despite the CME body residing in a slightly higher heliospheric environment. These findings suggest that small-scale fluctuations in the CME sheath are primarily driven by the complex interaction between the CME and the ambient solar wind, rather than solely by the heliospheric location. Additionally, the study highlights that small-scale fluctuations in CME sheath plasma are particularly remarkable, requiring further investigation to be fully understood. Complementing these results, graphical and statistical analyses of CME structures were performed using enhanced data processing and visualization tools. \section{Introduction}

The recent surge in gravitational wave (GW) detections has revealed numerous compact binary systems, revealing that black holes are more prevalent in the Galaxy than previously thought. Prior to the GW era, indirect evidence from X-ray binaries indicated that stellar-mass black holes form from core collapses of massive stars. The LIGO/Virgo observatories have identified two primary channels for binary black hole formation: binary stellar evolution (where massive stars form close pairs) and dynamical formation (where black holes originate from independent stellar evolution). Beyond stellar evolution, observational data support the existence of dark matter black holes within globular clusters and galactic centers. Specifically, (super-)massive black holes in galactic nuclei are believed to possess "feeder" regions containing numerous stellar-mass black holes that undergo dynamical interactions.

Thieullen demonstrated that a smooth projective variety $X$ with a full exceptional collection of identical type is of Picard type A precisely when it is a smooth quadric or a projective space. In this note, we extend that theorem. Specifically, for any integer $r \geq 2$, if $X$ possesses a full exceptional collection of mixed type $(r,n_1,\ldots,n_k)$, then $X$ is either a smooth quadric or a projective space provided that $\sum_{i=1}^k (2n_i-1) \leq r$. This confirms a question raised by Thieullen about the existence of full exceptional collections of varying types on varieties of Picard type A beyond projective spaces and smooth quadrics. Our proof builds upon Thieullen's work on uniformly generated collections and employs an explicit calculation of the cohomology of line bundles on smooth quadrics. We also generalize Thieullen's propositions to construct examples of Fano varieties featuring full exceptional collections of arbitrary types. Furthermore, we investigate the existence of full exceptional collections of uniform type matching the first Chern class of $X$ within the derived category of coherent sheaves $\mathbf D^b(\mathrm{qcoh} X)$, thereby answering a question by Thieullen. We conclude by examining Thieullen's open problem: whether the derived category of vector bundles $\mathbf D^b(\mathrm{vec} X)$ is equivalent to $\mathbf D^b(\mathrm{qcoh} X)$ for any Fano $X$ possessing a full exceptional collection of mixed types, a scenario that appears highly unlikely. We verify Thieullen's conjecture in specific instances: it holds true when $X$ is a smooth quadric, and it is sufficient to check the case where $X$ is a projective space. This confirms Thieullen's conjecture for all previously known examples of Fano varieties with full exceptional collections. We also discuss related open problems.

Recent progress in numerical methods for simulating atom-light interactions has opened new avenues for exploring these frontier phenomena. Simulation research at this level not only enhances our comprehension of fundamental atomic physics but also serves as a vital bridge between theoretical models and experimental validation. As experimental capabilities advance and more intricate physical effects emerge, the relevance of these simulations will increasingly align with actual laboratory conditions. This paper underscores the current state of the art in time-resolved experimental and simulation investigations of fundamental atomic phenomena and future directions. Specifically, we will examine simulations of attosecond phenomena involving both single-electron and multi-electron atomic systems.

The rapid advancement of experimental techniques has opened new frontiers in attosecond science and technology. Attosecond physics has been in close conversation with laser physics for decades, and this paper provides an overview of essential laser physics aspects that enable attosecond manipulation of atomic electrons. We begin by summarizing the current state of the art in attosecond light sources, which have progressed rapidly in recent years. We then discuss laser propagation and focus issues that have been critical in the early development of attosecond sources and remain relevant today. Following this, we examine how attosecond light sources are influenced by interaction conditions, such as the intensity and wavelength of driving laser fields, as well as propagation and focus effects that may have impacted experimental results. This section also addresses fundamental questions regarding attosecond pulse measurement and characterization. Finally, we provide an overview of experimental attosecond light sources, highlighting key challenges that serve as a guide for the design and implementation of next-generation sources that will drive future experimental science and technology.

Over the last decade, observing and controlling electron motion has been a primary goal in atomic physics. Driven by significant experimental and theoretical advancements, attosecond science has matured into a well-established field with clear future prospects. This progress has been made possible through sophisticated experimental setups and compelling theoretical insights, often supported by state-of-the-art simulation research. This final section provides an overview of experimental attosecond light sources and their interpretation through atom-light simulations and models. It begins by discussing experimental results and initial data analysis methods for time-resolved spectroscopy of atomic electrons. Subsequently, the specific roles of simulations and theoretical models at various stages of research are identified and highlighted. Current methods for dealing with partially observed data in complex networks rely on integrating statistical models with data-specific preprocessing steps, such as handling network sparsity and symmetry, which limits their applicability to diverse models and techniques.

To address this, we propose a Data Augmentation approach for partially observed complex networks. Treating the network structure as a collection of data points enables the application of statistical techniques and machine learning models to imperfect data through a unified interface. Our approach utilizes a Latent Block Model to achieve structural compression and maximize information gain from limited observations. We provide theoretical insights into the method and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations on both synthetic and real datasets. Furthermore, we extend the method to incorporate prior knowledge and examine various applications, including community detection, link prediction, and network completion. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/danielasigurd/COBAN. Lines Code.

Many existing text classification models depend on large-scale, well-annotated datasets. However, in practical scenarios, high domain specificity often necessitates custom classifiers, and gathering sufficient labeled data is frequently impractical. To address this, we explore domain adaptation for text classification. Our analysis reveals that while previous domain adaptation methods assume statistical distributions remain constant while labels shift, these assumptions are often invalid because label changes can imply fundamental distributional shifts. We examine four domain adaptation strategies for classification: 1) unsupervised, 2) semi-supervised, 3) weakly supervised, and 4) semi-supervised with label propagation. Through experiments on six Chinese news classification tasks across six datasets, we evaluate and compare these approaches. We also analyze how training set size, label noise, and feature extraction methods affect classification performance. Our results show that domain adaptation can enhance classification accuracy, with semi-supervised strategies outperforming supervised baselines when using 10% of the training data. Performance degrades gradually as the training set grows, remaining within 3% accuracy loss up to approximately 30% of the full dataset size. Among specific techniques, label propagation outperforms other semi-supervised approaches, while weakly supervised learning excels over standard unsupervised methods. Finally, we demonstrate that combining word2vec features with domain-specific terms yields the best results. The source code for our system is available at: https://github.com/zengrui1994/da-text-classification.

By applying temporal redundancy reasoning to this graph model, we introduce the Reducible Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN), an adaptive framework capable of optimizing GCN computations across three phases: forward propagation, backward propagation, and memory allocation. Unlike traditional Trojan attacks that embed small, insignificant patterns onto clean host images, our approach treats triggers as complete images representing semantically relevant object classes. Because the backdoored classifier learns to generalize on object classes rather than trigger pixels, these triggers remain effective even when resized or distorted. Furthermore, the method remains robust against many traditional transfer attacks, allowing for cross-dataset Trojan insertion. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate the superiority of our approach, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of performance on common benchmark datasets to illustrate the severe risks this attack poses to real-world AI systems. To our knowledge, this work represents the first image-level host-free Trojan attack utilizing semantic triggers. Consequently, our method not only surpasses state-of-the-art techniques but also marks a new era in AI model poisoning. Final evaluations emphasize the necessity of more rigorous testing for AI models, alongside model updates and safeguards, to ensure robustness against this emerging threat. Importantly, our approach has practical applications in legitimate scenarios, such as enabling contactless access control systems. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ai4j/SETR.

While transfer learning has gained significant popularity as a strategy to address this issue, recent research indicates that merely pretraining on a high-resource language is insufficient to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Consequently, low-resource languages must be incorporated during fine-tuning to mitigate potential negative transfer effects. However, effective transfer heavily relies on aligning latent representations across languages that correspond to identical phonetic content, a challenge that is particularly difficult to address when comprehensive human annotations are unavailable. This paper introduces a novel technique called Cross-lingual Contrastive Structure Mining (CCSM), which minimizes the discrepancy between latent representations of adjacent time frames in pre-trained and target languages to facilitate successful transfer. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach enables the achievement of state-of-the-art ASR performance for several low-resource languages using only small-scale pre-trained models. Listener evaluations further confirm that the generated embeddings closely mirror human-perceived audio content, validating the method's ability to capture consistent cross-lingual representations and effectively avoiding negative transfer. Overall, our approach significantly outperforms previous methods by substantially reducing the amount of pre-training data required, thereby making ASR more accessible to low-resource languages. Additionally, the code is publicly available at https://github.com/soi-uea/ccsm. Keywords: Automatic Speech Recognition, Transfer Learning, Embedding, Embedding Mining.

19) introduced a novel testing framework for diverse model classes within causal mediation analysis, assessing them against an exact hypothesis test based on a specific representation of the model class known as the mapping. This testing approach offers a compelling alternative dimension within the landscape of causal inference. This paper presents a framework generating counterexamples to disprove claims regarding the mapping of a given model class. Distinct from the testing framework by Gourdeau et al. (2019), this method avoids statistical estimation and hypothesis testing; instead, it constructs counterexamples using only the structural specifications of the model class. Distinctly, counterexample generation is representation-resistant. Counterexample generation constitutes a new benchmark in program verification for quantitative properties over discrete data. Furthermore, it enables the creation of a novel complexity measure for model classes concerning causal mediation analysis, defined as the minimum number of components required to approximate the mapping of a specific model class. This measure characterizes the difficulty in learning a causal model that remains faithful to the underlying data-generating process. Our learning algorithm is evaluated against counterexamples derived from the model classes under investigation. This approach represents the first learning method capable of achieving two primary objectives simultaneously: (i) learning a causal model class that aligns with the data, and (ii) learning a causal model that is faithful to the data-generating process. Finally, we introduce a metric to quantify faithfulness in empirical causal estimates, derived from the distance between the estimated mapping and the true data-generating process mapping. This faithfulness metric constitutes a new benchmark in empirical process theory for learning models that are both consistent with and faithful to the data-generating process. The paper concludes by examining faithfulness in the context of empirical causal inference. Our findings indicate that learning empirical causal models using this approach yields significantly more faithful causal estimates compared to existing methods in the literature. The code and data required to reproduce these results are accessible through a public GitHub repository. The public arXiv version of this paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.00871.
